### 1. Introduction With over 35% of global CO2 emissions and more than 40% of total energy use attributed to it, the construction industry stands as one of the most resource- and emission-intensive sectors worldwide \ [1, 2\]. The widespread acceptance of concrete as a popular building material is primarily due to its accessibility, cost-effectiveness, functionality, and ease of use \ [3, 4\]. Every year, roughly 30 billion tons of concrete are produced globally, contributing to about 3% of the world’s energy consumption and approximately 8% of total greenhouse gas emissions \ [5\]. The aggregate forms the more significant part of concrete, ranging from 60% to 70%, and is mainly made from natural and nonrenewable materials \ [6\]. Recycling coarse aggregates into regular concrete production in the cement industry has recently gained significance as part of the drive for circularity \ [7, 8\]. This trend has occurred primarily due to the need for a solution to reducing environmental impacts and the exhaustion of resources as natural coarse aggregates have increasingly taken the spotlight \ [9\]. In 2020, around 26 Gt of concrete was consumed globally, corresponding to some 20 Gt of aggregates \ [10\]. This immense demand, therefore, makes a strong case for developing sustainable means of concrete production. However, this transition carries a considerable number of challenges because of the variability in the quality of recycled concrete aggregate (RCA) \ [11\]. The production of ceramic tiles has doubled in the last few years, going from 8581 million m2 produced around the globe in 2009 to 16,093 million m2 in 2020 \ [12\]. Spain is the top producer of ceramic tiles in the European Union and the second largest worldwide, with 415 million m2 of ceramic tiles exported in 2020, representing 81.4% of the total production. The reuse of CTW contributes to circular economy strategies by decreasing reliance on virgin raw materials and mitigating the environmental impacts associated with landfill disposal \ [13\]. Construction and demolition activities occur globally, accounting for more than 75% of total waste generation \ [14\]. In addition, ceramic materials comprise approximately 54% of the waste from construction and demolition works \ [15\]. Because ceramics are brittle and easily break during production, transport, and installation, their use in building and structural construction is growing \ [16\]. Examples include tiles, electrical insulators, sanitary fittings, and other ceramic objects. Roughly 75% of all garbage produced worldwide results from construction and demolition materials \ [17\]. An advantageous type of recycling is collecting waste materials as raw inputs for producing corresponding virgin products \ [18\]. Given that CTW has the potential for sustainable construction material recycling, its integration into ceramic tiles has gained popularity. For example, CTW is utilized for paving bricks, porcelain tiles, un-few fired bricks, and foam ceramics \ [18\]. CTW has excellent potential to be used as a sustainable construction material in producing Ultra-High-Performance Concrete (UHPC) together with seawater concrete and additional construction materials \ [19\]. Implementing CTW materials in construction works would drive urban sustainability while decreasing waste production and directly help achieve targets under SDGs 11 and 12 from the United Nations \ [20\]. In their experiments, Poon and Chan \ [21\] replaced 20% of natural sand with finely crushed brick or tile waste in concrete and compared conventional vs. double mixing methods. This replacement slightly reduced the density of the concrete (e.g., control: 2390 kg/m3, brick mix: 2340 kg/m3, tile mix: 2370 kg/m3). The double mixing method increased compressive strength, with tile aggregate concrete achieving 55.3 MPa at 28 days—21.5% higher than conventional mixing. All mixes met the 45 MPa target strength, and drying shrinkage stayed under 0.075%, showing they are suitable for general applications. Tanash et al. \ [22\], exploring the use of ceramic waste, found that concrete with coarse ceramic aggregate had a higher compressive strength than the control, and its strength increased beyond 28 days. Elçi \ [23\] investigated employing 100% crushed wall and floor tile waste as fine and coarse aggregate replacements in concrete. The study compared their performance to a conventional limestone aggregate. Concrete made with wall tile aggregate (WTA) showed a significantly lower performance, with a fresh density 20% lower (1670 kg/m3 vs. 2377 kg/m3) and splitting tensile strength reduced by 15.6% (2.70 MPa vs. 3.20 MPa) at 28 days. In contrast, floor tile concrete (FTC) performed closer to limestone concrete (LSC), with only 14% lower fresh density (2036 kg/m3) and slightly higher splitting tensile strength (3.31 MPa vs. 3.20 MPa). While tile aggregates had a higher water absorption capacity (WTA: 18.57%, FTC: 12.46%, LSC: 6.06%), FTC offered a comparable mechanical strength, suggesting its potential as a sustainable aggregate alternative. Medeiros et al. \ [24\] studied eco-friendly concrete made using porcelain polishing and scheelite wastes, performing microstructural analysis to see how these materials impact concrete’s properties. Their research contributes to a broader understanding of how various waste materials can be integrated into concrete formulations to improve sustainability. Koushkbaghi et al. \ [25\] investigated the incorporation of RCA and rice husk ash (RHA) in concrete mixtures. When RCA entirely replaced the natural aggregate, the splitting tensile strength decreased by 22.2% in mixes without fibers and by 14.7% in those containing fibers. In fibrous mixes containing 20% RHA, tensile strength experienced only slight reductions of 2.2% at 28 days and 5.6% at 90 days, highlighting the positive effect of RHA on the fiber–matrix interface. Keshavarz and Mostofinejad \ [26\] conducted an experimental study on the use of porcelain and red ceramic waste as partial replacements for coarse aggregates in concrete. A total of 65 specimens were tested for compressive, tensile, and flexural strength, as well as water absorption. The results showed that porcelain significantly enhanced the concrete’s mechanical properties, improving compressive strength by 41% and flexural strength by 67%. However, both porcelain and red ceramic increased water absorption (54% for porcelain aggregate concrete, compared to 91% for brick aggregate concrete). Juan-Valdés et al. \ [27\] evaluated concrete mixes where natural coarse aggregates were partially replaced with recycled ceramic aggregates. The study included a control mix (using only natural aggregates) and a recycled mix (RC-RA). Mechanical strength, density, porosity, and microstructural analysis revealed that the recycled concrete achieved compressive strengths at 28 days equal to or exceeding those of conventional concrete. Additionally, it exhibited a more refined pore structure, confirming its potential as a sustainable construction material. Mousavi et al. \ [28\] examined the use of recycled ceramic aggregates from waste tiles and sanitary ware (CS) as partial replacements for natural coarse aggregates in high-strength concrete (HSC). Seven mixes with replacement levels ranging from 0 to 30% were tested for slump, compressive strength, water absorption, and chloride penetration. The study found that 20% CTW replacement improved mechanical strength, while 10% CS replacement enhanced durability. However, higher replacement levels led to increased water absorption and chloride ingress. The authors concluded that ceramic waste can be effectively and sustainably used to produce HSC (≥60.7 MPa), with optimal performance at 10–20% replacement—offering environmental benefits without compromising structural integrity. Although CTW has been widely studied as a sustainable material in concrete, most research to date has focused on its use as a fine aggregate or at low replacement levels for natural coarse aggregates \ [21, 23, 29\]. There is limited investigation into the use of CTW as a full or partial substitute for brick chips, which are commonly used as coarse aggregates in many developing countries. This gap is significant, as brick chips possess distinct physical properties—such as a higher porosity and lower density compared to natural stone—which may influence performance outcomes. Moreover, high replacement levels of CTW (above 40% by mass) remain underexplored, and a few existing studies report inconsistent results regarding strength and durability performance \ [23, 29\]. Direct comparative analyses between CTW and brick aggregate concrete are particularly scarce. While some studies have examined basic durability indicators like water absorption \ [23\], more comprehensive assessments of long-term performance—including shrinkage, freeze–thaw resistance, and sulfate attack—are lacking. Similarly, despite frequent references to the environmental benefits of CTW, quantitative evaluations such as cost–benefit analyses and environmental impact assessments are still rare \ [30\]. These research gaps limit a full understanding of CTW’s potential as a sustainable coarse aggregate, particularly in contexts where brick aggregate concrete is prevalent. Ceramic tile waste (CTW), particularly porcelain based, exhibits superior physical and chemical properties compared to other recycled aggregates such as crushed concrete or red ceramic. These advantages include higher particle density, lower porosity, and a more uniform mineral composition \ [23, 26, 30\], all of which contribute to improved mechanical strength and durability when incorporated into concrete. These benefits have been confirmed in recent experimental studies \ [23, 26\]. Building upon this prior research, the present study demonstrates that CTW concrete—particularly at a 40% replacement level—outperforms conventional brick aggregate concrete in terms of mechanical performance. This study aimed to address several of the previously identified research gaps by evaluating the effects of incorporating CTW as a partial replacement for brick chips in concrete at replacement levels of 20%, 40%, and 70%—higher than those commonly reported in the literature. The focus on brick chips, rather than natural coarse aggregates, reflects construction practices in many developing regions, where brick aggregate is widely used. This enhances the practical relevance and applicability of the findings. A series of experimental tests were conducted to assess key concrete properties, including compressive strength, split tensile strength, unit weight, water absorption, and modulus of elasticity, to better understand the performance of CTW as a coarse aggregate. The results of this study show that moderate replacement levels, particularly at 40%, enhanced both the strength and durability of the concrete compared to the control mix containing only brick aggregate. At higher replacement levels (e.g., 70%), performance remained comparable to traditional brick aggregate concrete. In addition, the study highlights the sustainability benefits of using CTW, such as reducing construction waste sent to landfills and conserving natural resources.

**The Historical Evolution of Plant-Based Culinary Traditions in Mediterranean Cultures**  

**Abstract**  
This paper investigates the development of plant-based culinary traditions within Mediterranean cultures, tracing their origins from antiquity through to contemporary fusion cuisine. It examines the interplay of trade, religious customs, and seasonal ingredient availability in shaping dietary preferences, with particular attention to how these sociocultural factors have influenced the continuity and transformation of recipes and cooking methods. By synthesizing historical records, archaeological findings, and ethnographic studies, the research illuminates the enduring role of plant-based foods in the Mediterranean gastronomic identity.  

**Introduction**  
The Mediterranean basin has long been recognized as a nexus of cultural exchange and agricultural abundance. Its culinary traditions, deeply rooted in the cultivation of grains, legumes, vegetables, fruits, and herbs, reflect millennia of adaptation to local climates and resources. While animal products have been present, plant-based foods have occupied a central role in daily sustenance and ceremonial meals alike. This study traces the historical trajectory of these plant-based traditions, identifying key inflection points where sociocultural forces altered taste preferences and cooking methods.  

**Plant-Based Diets in Antiquity**  
Archaeobotanical evidence from sites in Greece, Italy, and the Levant indicates that cereals such as wheat and barley, alongside pulses like lentils and chickpeas, formed the staple diet in the Bronze Age and Classical periods [1]. Olive oil, a defining feature of Mediterranean cuisine, served both culinary and ritual purposes, while figs, grapes, and pomegranates provided seasonal sweetness. Trade across the Aegean and along Phoenician routes introduced new plant species, including saffron and certain legumes, which diversified local diets [2].  

Cooking methods in antiquity emphasized simplicity, often involving boiling, baking, or grilling over open flames. Plant-based stews were common, enriched with herbs such as oregano, thyme, and coriander. The philosophical schools of ancient Greece, notably the Pythagoreans, advocated for vegetarian regimens on ethical and spiritual grounds, further embedding plant-based diets in certain strata of society [3].  

**Religious Customs and Culinary Continuity**  
From late antiquity into the medieval period, religious customs exerted significant influence on dietary practices. Christian fasting periods, such as Lent, restricted the consumption of meat, dairy, and eggs, prompting the development of elaborate plant-based dishes to maintain nutritional adequacy and culinary satisfaction [4]. Similarly, Islamic dietary laws in North Africa and the Levant encouraged the use of legumes, grains, and vegetables, particularly during Ramadan when pre-dawn and sunset meals required nutrient-dense yet permissible foods.  

Seasonal ingredient availability reinforced the reliance on plant-based staples. The Mediterranean climate, with its hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters, favored crops like olives, grapes, and hardy greens. Preservation techniques—including drying, pickling, and fermenting—ensured year-round access to plant-based components, which in turn shaped regional recipe repertoires.  

**Trade Routes and Ingredient Diffusion**  
The expansion of trade during the medieval and early modern periods introduced new botanical elements to Mediterranean cuisines. The arrival of rice from Asia via Arab traders transformed pilaf and risotto traditions [5]. The Columbian exchange brought tomatoes, peppers, and beans from the Americas, which rapidly integrated into local diets and became emblematic of Mediterranean cooking by the 18th century.  

These introductions prompted adaptations in existing plant-based recipes. For example, the Sicilian caponata incorporated New World vegetables into a framework of sweet-and-sour flavoring inherited from Arab culinary influence. In the Levant, tomato-based stews supplanted older pomegranate reductions in certain contexts, while retaining the legume and grain base.  

**Contemporary Fusion and Globalization**  
In the modern era, Mediterranean plant-based cuisine has engaged with global culinary trends, fostering fusion dishes that blend traditional ingredients with techniques from Asia, the Americas, and beyond. Chefs in Athens, Barcelona, and Beirut experiment with quinoa, tofu, and exotic spices, while maintaining core Mediterranean flavor profiles rooted in olive oil, fresh herbs, and seasonal produce.  

Health-conscious movements and sustainability concerns have further elevated the visibility of plant-based Mediterranean diets in international gastronomy. Contemporary cookbooks and culinary schools increasingly emphasize traditional plant-based recipes as both nutritionally balanced and culturally rich. This renewed interest has catalyzed preservation efforts for heirloom crop varieties and artisanal preparation methods, ensuring continuity amid innovation.  

**Conclusion**  
The historical evolution of plant-based culinary traditions in the Mediterranean reflects a dynamic interplay of environmental conditions, religious customs, and intercultural exchange. From ancient grain-and-legume staples to modern fusion cuisine, plant-based foods have persisted as a cornerstone of the region’s gastronomic identity. The adaptability of these traditions to new ingredients and contexts underscores their resilience and enduring appeal, making them a vital subject for ongoing culinary and cultural scholarship.

[2] Horden, P., & Purcell, N. (2000). *The Corrupting Sea: A Study of Mediterranean History*. Blackwell.  
[3] Wilkins, J., Harvey, D., & Dobson, M. (1994). *Food in the Ancient World*. Blackwell.

# A Complete Guide to Using Waterproofing Sprays for Outdoor Camping Gear

When you’re relying on your camping gear to keep you dry and comfortable, waterproofing sprays can be a practical way to extend the life of fabrics and maintain their performance in wet conditions. These sprays work by creating a protective layer on the surface of textiles, helping them repel water while preserving breathability. In this guide, we’ll cover the fundamentals of waterproofing sprays, step-by-step application techniques, and tips for ensuring your gear remains both weather-resistant and comfortable.

---

## Understanding Waterproofing Sprays

Waterproofing sprays are typically formulated to bond with synthetic and natural fibers, forming a hydrophobic barrier. This barrier allows water droplets to bead and roll off instead of soaking into the fabric. Many sprays are designed for use on tents, jackets, backpacks, and even sleeping bags, and can be applied in a home environment with minimal equipment.

While formulations vary, most modern sprays aim to balance water resistance with breathability—critical for outdoor gear, since trapped moisture from perspiration can lead to discomfort and reduced insulation performance.

---

## Preparing Your Gear

Before applying any waterproofing spray, proper preparation is key:

1. **Clean the Item Thoroughly**  
   Dirt, body oils, and residues can interfere with the spray’s ability to bond to fibers. Wash fabric items according to manufacturer instructions, and allow them to dry completely.

2. **Check Compatibility**  
   Read the spray’s label to ensure it’s suitable for the fabric type. Some materials, such as certain coated nylons, may already have a factory-applied waterproof layer that doesn’t require additional treatment.

3. **Work in a Well-Ventilated Area**  
   Sprays can produce fine mist and vapors, so apply them outdoors or in a space with good airflow.

---

## Step-by-Step Application Technique

1. **Shake the Can Well**  
   This ensures the active ingredients are evenly mixed.

2. **Hold the Spray at the Recommended Distance**  
   Typically, 6–8 inches from the fabric surface. Spraying too close can oversaturate the material, while spraying too far may result in uneven coverage.

3. **Apply in Even, Overlapping Passes**  
   Move the spray in a consistent sweeping motion. Overlap each pass slightly to avoid missed spots.

4. **Focus on High-Exposure Areas**  
   Pay extra attention to seams, shoulders, and other parts of gear that see the most rain or contact with wet surfaces.

5. **Allow Proper Drying Time**  
   Most sprays require several hours to cure. Avoid using or packing the gear until it’s fully dry.

---

## Maximizing Fabric Breathability

One common concern with waterproofing is the potential reduction in breathability. Here are some tips to help maintain comfort:

- **Avoid Overapplication**  
  Excess spray can clog the fabric’s pores, impeding airflow. Follow the recommended amount on the label.

- **Choose Breathable Formulations**  
  Some sprays are engineered to maintain or restore the water-repellent finish without sealing the fabric completely.

- **Reapply as Needed, Not Excessively**  
  Frequent treatments can build up layers that hinder performance. Monitor your gear’s water resistance and reapply only when water stops beading.

---

## Maintenance and Longevity

Waterproofing sprays are not permanent; exposure to abrasion, UV light, and repeated washing will diminish their effectiveness over time. To extend the protection:

- **Spot Clean When Possible**  
  Instead of full washes, remove dirt from small areas with a damp cloth.

- **Store Gear Properly**  
  Keep treated items in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight.

- **Re-treat Seasonally**  
  For gear used heavily in wet conditions, a seasonal refresh helps maintain optimal performance.

---

## Final Thoughts

Applied correctly, waterproofing sprays can breathe new life into your outdoor camping gear, helping you stay dry without sacrificing comfort. By following these preparation and application steps, and being mindful of breathability, you can ensure your equipment performs reliably in challenging environments. Whether you’re braving a rainy trail, setting up camp by a misty lake, or trekking through morning dew, well-treated gear can make all the difference in your outdoor experience.

* Community function guilds group species based on a specific function or niche that they fill in the garden. Examples of this type of guild include plants that attract a particular beneficial insect or plants that restore nitrogen to the soil. These types of guilds are aimed at solving specific problems which may arise in a garden, such as infestations of harmful insects and poor nutrition in the soil.  [30]
* Establishment guilds are commonly used when working to establish target species (the primary vegetables, fruits, herbs, etc. you want to be established in your garden) with the support of pioneer species (plants that will help the target species succeed). For example, in [ temperate climates ](/wiki/Temperate_climate "Temperate climate") , plants such as [ comfrey ](/wiki/Comfrey "Comfrey") (as a weed barrier and [ dynamic accumulator ](/wiki/Dynamic_accumulator "Dynamic accumulator") ), [ lupine ](/wiki/Lupine_\(flower\) "Lupine \(flower\)") (as a nitrogen fixer), and [ daffodil ](/wiki/Daffodil "Daffodil") (as a [ gopher ](/wiki/Gopher "Gopher") deterrent) can together form a guild for a fruit tree. As the tree matures, the support plants will likely eventually be shaded out and can be used as compost.  [30]
* Mature guilds form once your target species are established. For example, if the tree layer of your landscape closes its [ canopy ](/wiki/Canopy_\(biology\) "Canopy \(biology\)") , sun-loving support plants will be shaded out and die. Shade loving [ medicinal herbs ](/wiki/Medicinal_herbs "Medicinal herbs") such as [ ginseng ](/wiki/Ginseng "Ginseng") , [ Black Cohosh ](/wiki/Black_Cohosh "Black Cohosh") , and [ goldenseal ](/wiki/Goldenseal "Goldenseal") can be planted as an [ understory ](/wiki/Understory "Understory") .  [30]
* Mutual support guilds group species together that are complementary by working together and supporting each other. This guild may include a plant that fixes nitrogen, a plant that hosts insects that are predators to pests, and another plant that attracts pollinators.  [30]
* Resource partitioning guilds group species based on their abilities to share essential resources with one another through a process of niche differentiation. An example of this type of guild includes placing a [ fibrous- or shallow-rooted plant ](/wiki/Fibrous_root_system "Fibrous root system") next to a [ tap-rooted plant ](/wiki/Taproot "Taproot") so that they draw from different levels of soil nutrients.  [30]

To develop a deeper understanding of the lifecycle of EV batteries, it is
important to analyze the emission associated with different phases. Using NMC
cylindrical cells as an example, Ciez and Whitacre found that around 9 kg CO
2  e kg battery _ −  _ 1  is emitted during raw materials pre-processing and
battery manufacturing under the US average electricity grid. The biggest part
of the emission came from materials preparation accounting for more than 50%
of the emissions. If NMC pouch cell is used, the total emission increases to
almost 10 kg CO  2  e kg battery _ −  _ 1  while materials manufacturing still
contributes to more than 50% of the emission.  [34]  During the end-of-life
management phase, the refurbishing process adds little emission to the
lifecycle emission. The recycling process, on the other hand, as suggested by
Ciez and Whitacre emits a significant amount of GHG. As shown in the battery
recycling emission plot a and c, the emission of the recycling process varies
with the different recycling processes, different chemistry and different form
factor. Thus, the net emission avoided compared to not recycling also varies
with these factors. At a glance, as shown in the plot b and d, the direct
recycling process is the most ideal process for recycling pouch cell
batteries, while the hydrometallurgical process is most suitable for
cylindrical type battery. However, with the error bars shown, the best
approach cannot be picked with confidence. It is worth noting that for the
lithium iron phosphates (LFP) chemistry, the net benefit is negative. Because
LFP cells lacks cobalt and nickel which are expensive and energy intensive to
produce, it is more energetically efficient to mine. In general, in addition
to promoting the growth of a single sector, a more integrated effort should be
in place to reduce the lifecycle emission of EV batteries. A finite total
supply of rare earth material can apparently justify the need for recycling.
But the environmental benefit of recycling needs closer scrutiny. Based on
current recycling technology, the net benefit of recycling depends on the form
factors, the chemistry and the recycling process chosen.

**The Role of Boreal Forests in Global Carbon Sequestration: Chemical Processes, Climate Regulation, and Implications of Deforestation**  

---

**Abstract**  
Boreal forests constitute one of the largest terrestrial biomes and play a critical role in the global carbon cycle through substantial carbon sequestration in biomass and soils. This paper examines the chemical and ecological mechanisms underlying carbon storage in boreal ecosystems, with particular emphasis on Canadian and Scandinavian regions. Seasonal variations in carbon flux, biomass density metrics, and the consequences of deforestation for atmospheric CO₂ concentrations are analyzed through recent case studies. The findings highlight the importance of boreal forests as climate regulators and underscore the potential long-term impacts of anthropogenic disturbances on global carbon balance.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Boreal forests, spanning approximately 11% of the Earth's land surface, are characterized by coniferous dominance, cold climate adaptations, and extensive peatland systems [1]. Their vast expanse in Canada, Scandinavia, and Russia has positioned them as a major sink in the global carbon budget. Unlike tropical forests, boreal systems store a significant proportion of carbon in soils and below-ground biomass, making them uniquely sensitive to changes in temperature and moisture regimes. Understanding the chemical processes of carbon sequestration and the effects of deforestation is essential for predicting climate feedbacks in high-latitude ecosystems.

---

**2. Chemical Processes of Carbon Sequestration**  
Carbon sequestration in boreal forests occurs via photosynthesis, where atmospheric CO₂ is fixed into organic compounds by plant tissues. The generalized reaction:  

6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂  

is mediated by chlorophyll in coniferous needles and deciduous leaves. Seasonal variations in light availability drive fluctuations in photosynthetic rates, with maximum assimilation observed during late spring and early summer [2]. Carbon is stored in above-ground biomass (trunks, branches, foliage) and below-ground biomass (roots), as well as in soil organic matter derived from litter decomposition. Low temperatures and acidic soils slow microbial activity, resulting in long-term carbon retention in humus and peat layers.

---

**3. Biomass Density and Carbon Flux in Canadian and Scandinavian Boreal Zones**  
Field measurements in northern Ontario, Canada, indicate above-ground biomass densities averaging 90–120 Mg ha⁻¹, with soil organic carbon stocks exceeding 150 Mg ha⁻¹ in peat-rich areas [3]. In Scandinavian boreal forests, particularly in northern Sweden, biomass densities are slightly lower (80–110 Mg ha⁻¹) due to shorter growing seasons, but soil carbon reserves remain high, often surpassing 130 Mg ha⁻¹. Eddy covariance tower data reveal seasonal carbon flux patterns: net ecosystem exchange (NEE) values are negative (net uptake) during summer months and positive (net release) during winter dormancy, with annual net sequestration rates between 1.5–2.5 Mg C ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ [4].

---

**4. Climate Regulation Functions**  
Beyond carbon storage, boreal forests influence climate through albedo effects, evapotranspiration, and atmospheric moisture recycling. Dark coniferous canopies lower surface albedo, absorbing more solar radiation, while transpiration contributes to local and regional hydrological cycles. The balance between these processes determines whether boreal regions act as net coolers or warmers under different climatic scenarios. Elevated CO₂ concentrations from deforestation can amplify greenhouse effects, potentially offsetting cooling benefits from albedo changes.

---

**5. Effects of Deforestation on Atmospheric CO₂ Levels**  
Clearcutting, wildfire intensification, and pest outbreaks can release large quantities of stored carbon into the atmosphere. In Canadian boreal forests, deforestation events have been linked to immediate emissions of 50–70 Mg C ha⁻¹, with additional long-term losses from soil respiration once canopy cover is removed [5]. Scandinavian case studies show similar patterns, where land-use changes reduce carbon stocks and alter seasonal flux dynamics. The lag between biomass removal and soil carbon release underscores the importance of long-term monitoring to capture full climatic impacts.

---

**6. Conclusions**  
Boreal forests are integral to the stabilization of global atmospheric CO₂ concentrations through complex chemical and ecological processes. The interplay between biomass accumulation, soil carbon retention, and seasonal flux variations shapes their role as a major carbon sink. Evidence from Canadian and Scandinavian case studies demonstrates both the resilience and vulnerability of these systems in the face of deforestation and climate change. Preserving boreal forest integrity is essential for maintaining their climate regulation functions and mitigating anthropogenic carbon emissions.

---

**Cycling Tourism in Rural Europe: Economic Impacts and Emerging Trends**  
*Report*  

---

**Executive Summary**  
Cycling tourism has emerged as a significant contributor to rural economic development across Europe over the past two decades. This report examines current trends, regional case studies, and the mechanisms by which bike touring stimulates local economies. By analyzing spending patterns on lodging, dining, and cultural attractions, the study highlights both the direct and indirect benefits to rural communities, as well as strategic approaches for sustainable growth.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Rural Europe has long faced challenges related to depopulation, economic stagnation, and limited employment opportunities. In response, many regions have leveraged natural landscapes, historical sites, and cultural heritage to attract visitors. Cycling tourism—defined as leisure travel involving overnight stays and substantial use of bicycles for transport—has proven particularly effective in revitalizing rural economies. The combination of physical activity, scenic routes, and immersive local experiences appeals to a growing demographic seeking sustainable and authentic travel.

---

**2. Market Overview**  
According to data from the European Cyclists’ Federation (ECF, 2022), cycling tourism generates an estimated €44 billion annually across Europe. Rural regions account for a significant portion of this expenditure, as touring cyclists often prefer less congested roads and access to nature. The typical cycling tourist spends between €50 and €70 per day, excluding equipment purchases, with a notable emphasis on locally-owned services.

---

**3. Spending Patterns and Economic Impact**  

**3.1 Lodging**  
Cyclists tend to favor smaller, family-run accommodations such as guesthouses, bed-and-breakfasts, and rural hotels. This preference directly channels revenue into local hands rather than multinational chains. In Brittany, France, for example, cycling routes like the Vélodyssée have increased annual occupancy rates in rural lodgings by up to 25% during peak season.

**3.2 Dining**  
Expenditure on food and beverages is consistently high among cycling tourists, who require regular caloric intake during multi-day tours. Local restaurants, bakeries, and markets benefit from this demand. In Emilia-Romagna, Italy, cycling routes that connect historic towns have led to a measurable uptick in sales of regional specialties, from handmade pasta to artisanal cheeses.

**3.3 Cultural Attractions**  
Cyclists often seek out museums, historical sites, and cultural festivals along their routes. In the Danube region, cultural stops integrated into cycling itineraries have increased ticket sales for small museums by 40% in the past five years. This not only supports heritage preservation but also fosters cross-cultural exchange.

---

**4. Regional Case Studies**  

**4.1 The Greenways of Spain**  
Spain’s network of “Vías Verdes” has transformed disused railway lines into cycle-friendly trails. Rural towns along these routes report growth in small hospitality businesses and artisanal production. The Sierra de la Demanda Greenway, for instance, has spurred the opening of new hostels and craft shops catering exclusively to cyclists.

**4.2 The Baltic Sea Cycle Route**  
Stretching through rural coastal areas in Germany, Denmark, and Sweden, this route exemplifies cross-border collaboration. Local economies benefit not only from overnight stays but also from ferry services, bike repair shops, and guided tours. The economic multiplier effect is particularly strong where communities offer integrated packages combining cycling with local cultural experiences.

---

**5. Driving Factors Behind Growth**  
Several factors contribute to the ongoing expansion of cycling tourism in rural Europe:  
- **Infrastructure Investment:** Dedicated bike paths, signage, and safety measures increase accessibility.  
- **Sustainable Travel Trends:** Growing awareness of environmental impact encourages low-carbon travel options.  
- **Health and Wellness Appeal:** Cycling combines leisure with fitness, attracting a broad demographic.  
- **Digital Promotion:** Online route maps and booking platforms facilitate trip planning and increase visibility for rural destinations.

---

**6. Challenges and Opportunities**  
While the economic impact is clear, rural regions must address challenges such as seasonal fluctuations, infrastructure maintenance, and balancing tourism growth with environmental conservation. Opportunities include diversifying offerings (e.g., e-bike rentals to widen participation), developing themed routes (wine regions, historical trails), and fostering partnerships between local governments and private enterprises.

---

**7. Conclusion**  
Cycling tourism represents a sustainable and profitable avenue for rural economic revitalization in Europe. By capitalizing on natural scenery, cultural heritage, and community-driven hospitality, rural areas can attract a steady stream of visitors whose spending supports local businesses. Strategic investment in infrastructure, coupled with targeted marketing and cultural integration, will be key to sustaining and expanding these benefits in the years ahead.

---

**Local Neighborhoods Lead the Charge on Energy Efficiency Upgrades**  

*By Staff Reporter*  

In cities and towns across the country, residents are banding together to cut their electricity bills and shrink their carbon footprints through coordinated energy efficiency projects. These community-led initiatives, often organized by neighborhood associations or grassroots environmental groups, are proving that small-scale collaboration can yield significant results.  

One such example is the Green Blocks Program in Brookside, a mid-sized suburban neighborhood that has spent the past two years retrofitting dozens of homes with modern energy-saving technologies. The program began with a handful of volunteers conducting home energy audits, identifying common inefficiencies such as poor insulation, outdated lighting fixtures, and thermostats that failed to optimize heating and cooling schedules.  

**Retrofitting for Impact**  
The first phase of the initiative focused on improving insulation in older homes. Many properties in Brookside were built before modern building codes mandated higher insulation standards, leading to substantial heat loss in winter and heat gain in summer. Volunteers worked with local contractors to install high-quality wall and attic insulation, as well as weather-stripping for doors and windows. These upgrades have helped households maintain comfortable indoor temperatures with far less reliance on heating and cooling systems, translating into immediate energy savings.  

Lighting was the second major target. By replacing incandescent bulbs with LED fixtures, participating homes reduced lighting-related energy use by up to 80 percent. The switch not only lowers electricity consumption but also cuts maintenance costs, as LED bulbs last significantly longer than traditional ones. In some cases, residents pooled resources to purchase LED bulbs in bulk at discounted rates, further enhancing the economic benefits of the program.  

**Smart Technology Integration**  
A more recent phase introduced smart thermostats and energy monitoring devices. These technologies allow homeowners to program heating and cooling schedules, adjust settings remotely, and track energy usage in real time. In Brookside, many residents have reported that smart thermostats quickly adapt to household routines, reducing unnecessary heating and cooling when rooms are unoccupied.  

Neighborhood coordinator Elena Ruiz notes that the adoption of smart devices has been transformative: “It’s one thing to insulate a home and change the light bulbs, but giving residents the tools to see and control their energy use day-to-day really changes behavior. People become more conscious and proactive.”  

**Community Benefits Beyond Savings**  
While the primary goal has been to reduce electricity demand, the initiative has generated additional benefits. The collaborative nature of the project has strengthened community ties, with residents sharing knowledge, tools, and even labor to help each other complete upgrades. Several households have reported feeling more connected to their neighbors after working together on energy retrofits.  

Local utility companies have also taken notice. In Brookside, the regional power provider offered rebates for certain efficiency upgrades, further incentivizing participation. The reduced demand across the neighborhood has had a measurable effect on peak load times, potentially easing strain on the grid during hot summer afternoons.  

**Looking Ahead**  
Encouraged by the results, Brookside’s organizers plan to expand the program to nearby neighborhoods. Workshops on insulation techniques, LED installation, and smart thermostat programming are being scheduled for the coming months. The hope is that these grassroots efforts will inspire broader adoption of energy efficiency measures at the municipal level.  

Experts say that while large-scale renewable energy projects often capture headlines, localized efficiency improvements can be equally important in achieving sustainability goals. By lowering overall electricity demand, communities like Brookside not only reduce emissions but also make it easier for renewable sources to meet a greater share of the grid’s needs.  

As more neighborhoods embrace this model, the cumulative effect could be substantial—turning modest home upgrades into a powerful driver of environmental and economic resilience. In the words of Ruiz, “We’re showing that you don’t have to wait for big policy changes to make a difference. You can start right where you live, with the people you know, and together create lasting change.”

### The need for full production cycle analyses Most importantly, however, the felling of trees and the subsequent fate of the carbon sequestered in the wood needs to be considered (Ciais et al. 2008). As little as 50% of the actual tree biomass may be extracted during harvest; the remainder is left to decompose on site and within a few years returns as CO2 to the atmosphere (Korkiakoski et al. 2019; Leturcq 2020). After a tree is felled, much of its carbon can be stored in wood products. The processing of raw wood for product is estimated to produce (1) waste wood residues and (2) short-lived products (bioenergy, pellets, and pulp and paper (Jasinevičius 2018) of ∼40–60% being subject to fast carbon release (Sokka et al. 2015). Yet a simple carbon balance does not tell the whole story; unlike the carbon stock in soil and peat, not everything made out of wood is climate neutral (Leturcq 2020). As a rule, for a long-lasting product made out of 80-year old wood to be climate cooling, the wood should not be discarded and burnt for at least 40 years after harvest. A product made from 40-year old wood would need to remain for at least 20 years after harvest (Guest et al. 2013; Galimshina et al. 2022). Long-lived harvested wood products are actually quite rare, and harvesting does reduce the total amount of carbon stored in the forest (Soimakallio et al. 2022). In assessing the GHG balance of peatland forestry, complete harvest cycles should be taken into account. Such data are simply absent at the moment. Since trees grow slowly, no measurements of full growth cycles are yet available and results that span longer time periods are derived from the investigation of chronosequences. Certainly, more chronosequence work is needed, but measurements must be made over multiple years so that variations in weather and other environmental conditions can be integrated into the models. As Vanguelova et al. ( 2018) have expressed: “There is a clear need for long-term studies using different planting ages (chronosequence studies) to ensure robust results when evaluating the impacts of afforestation and restocking on soil carbon stocks, as short-term impact studies are likely to provide misleading conclusions.” Overall, Finland's land use sector, for instance, seems to have gradually transitioned from being a CO2 sink to a source (Statistics Finland 2022b) driven by increased demand for wood products, slower increase in growing stock, and rising emissions from soil organic matter and litter in drained peat-based forest soils. Siljander et al. ( 2022) have suggested that the fastest way to strengthen carbon sinks in Finland is to reduce logging, and the Finnish Nature Panel has recommended, among other things, the rewetting and restoration of wetlands and peatlands (Lång et al. 2022). ### Additional possible effects of drained peatland forestry Peatland forestry on drained sites is more prone to wildfires (Kohlenberg et al. 2018), which will become more frequent and severe in times of climate change with more frequent and more intense droughts in the boreal zone (Walker et al. 2019). Boreal forests in North America have turned from a net sink to a net source of GHG in recent years (Zhao et al. 2021), primarily due to more frequent and more severe fires (Zheng et al. 2023). In addition to the carbon loss from burnt wood, as well as substantial carbon losses from burnt and burning peat layers, should be considered, including the waterborne carbon losses (Liu et al. 2023). In countries with a relatively high density of forest roads, such as Finland, the severity of forest fires on peatland could be increased. This is because large drained peatland areas with forest often have a much lower density of roads compared to areas with mineral ground, thereby making it more challenging to control fires in these peatland regions. In addition to GHG exchange, the change in albedo and the release of aerosols, together with the lateral exchange of carbon and nitrogen, all add to the total climate effect of ecosystems (Billett et al. 2010). Increased tree cover decreases the albedo effect compared to a treeless mire (Lohila et al. 2010), which leads to local warming (Gao et al. 2014). However, forests are also large sources of biogenic volatile organic compounds (BVOC) and thus may have a considerable cooling impact on the climate (Tunved et al. 2006). In the boreal zone, this impact is similar in magnitude, but opposite to that of the albedo (Kalliokoski et al. 2020). Aside from site-related atmospheric impacts, forestry on peatland may also have negative impacts on water storage capacity, water quality and nutrients runoff, including loss of organic matter via fluvial pathways, which is subsequently mineralised and the carbon partially returned to the atmosphere (Evans et al. 2016). Rewetting of drained peatlands can also lead to considerable amounts of nitrogen and phosphorus leaching ( _e.g._, Koskinen et al. 2017) but the nutrient-sink function can be rapidly recovered provided further restoration management is implemented (Zak and McInnes 2022). The loss in water storage capacity due to the loss of pore space caused by drainage can manifest itself in greater variations in stream flow and water quality for downstream aquatic ecosystems (Flynn et al. 2021). Intense rainfall events are predicted to increase under climate warming, which can cause mid-term flooding leading to the die-back of trees caused by increased hydrological instability. Indeed, more research to evaluate the trade-off values of wood production, carbon sequestration and emissions, and water storage of natural, drained, and rewetted peatlands like it has been recently published by Makrickas et al. ( 2023) is urgently required (Manton et al. 2021).

**Shredded White Paper: Creative Craft Projects for Home and Hobby**  

If you’ve ever found yourself with bags of shredded white paper and wondered how to put it to good use, you’re in luck. Shredded paper is a surprisingly versatile material for crafting—lightweight, easy to manipulate, and capable of taking on a wide range of textures depending on how it’s prepared. Whether you’re looking to make intricate papier-mâché models or create stylish, decorative packaging filler, the possibilities are endless.  

---

### 1. Preparing Shredded Paper for Craft Use  

Before diving into projects, take a few minutes to prepare your paper properly. The key to successful crafting lies in achieving the right texture and preventing clumping.  

- **Shred Finely:** Use a cross-cut shredder for smaller, more uniform pieces. Long strips can be useful for some projects, but fine shreds blend and mold more easily for papier-mâché.  
- **Separate and Fluff:** If your paper has been compressed, run your fingers through it to loosen the fibers. This helps prevent clumping and ensures even absorption of glue or paste.  
- **Dry Thoroughly:** If the paper has been stored in a humid environment, spread it out in a thin layer and let it air-dry before use. Damp paper tends to stick together and can cause uneven textures.  

---

### 2. Papier-Mâché Models  

Papier-mâché is a classic craft technique that transforms shredded paper into sturdy, sculptable forms.  

**Materials Needed:**  
- Finely shredded paper  
- Adhesive paste (made from flour and water or PVA glue diluted with water)  
- Mold or armature (balloons, cardboard frames, wire structures)  

**Steps:**  
1. **Create the Paste:** Mix your adhesive paste until smooth.  
2. **Soak and Blend:** Dip the shredded paper into the paste and knead lightly to saturate. For smoother surfaces, blend the paper and paste into a pulp using a hand mixer.  
3. **Apply in Layers:** Press the paper mixture onto your mold in thin layers, allowing each layer to partially dry before adding the next.  
4. **Shape and Smooth:** Use your fingers or a spatula to smooth the surface as you go.  
5. **Dry Completely:** Let the finished model dry for at least 24–48 hours.  

Papier-mâché can be painted, varnished, or decorated once dry, making it perfect for masks, bowls, or figurines.  

---

### 3. Decorative Packaging Filler  

Shredded white paper can instantly elevate gift wrapping or product packaging. Its clean, neutral appearance works with any color scheme, and it provides cushioning for fragile items.  

**Tips for Perfect Packaging Filler:**  
- **Fluff for Volume:** Lightly toss the shreds by hand to create a soft, voluminous texture.  
- **Mix in Accents:** Add metallic foil shreds, colored paper, or raffia for visual interest.  
- **Avoid Compaction:** Store filler loosely in a box or bag; compressed shreds lose their airy look.  

This approach works beautifully for gift baskets, subscription boxes, and special event favors.  

---

### 4. Textured Art and Collage  

Shredded paper can add unique dimension to mixed media art. By layering shreds over painted surfaces or embedding them into glue washes, you can create tactile backgrounds and patterns.  

**Technique Ideas:**  
- **Layer with Acrylics:** Brush a thin layer of acrylic paint onto a canvas, sprinkle shreds on top, and press gently. Once dry, paint over them for a raised texture.  
- **Glue Wash Effects:** Mix shreds into a diluted glue solution and spread across paper or cardboard for a rough, organic surface.  
- **Stencil Embedding:** Place a stencil over your work, spread glue, add shreds, then lift the stencil to reveal a patterned relief.  

---

### 5. Avoiding Clumping and Maintaining Texture  

Clumping is the most common obstacle when working with shredded paper. To prevent it:  
- Work with small batches at a time.  
- Keep paper dry until the moment you apply adhesive.  
- Use tools like wide-tooth combs or mesh sieves to separate fibers before use.  

---

**Final Thoughts**  

Shredded white paper is more than just scrap—it’s a flexible, creative medium for a variety of home projects. By preparing it thoughtfully and experimenting with techniques, you can transform everyday paper into art, décor, and functional craft materials. Whether you’re sculpting, decorating, or cushioning a gift, the humble shred can be the foundation of something beautiful.

# Denmark data center to warm local community At Facebook, we aim to minimize our energy, emissions and water impact, while embracing the responsibility and opportunity to impact the world beyond our operations. # The opportunity When we announced the construction of our Odense Data Center in 2017, we were determined to build one of the most advanced, energy-efficient data centers in the world. The new facility will feature our latest hyperefficient hardware, cooled using outdoor air through indirect evaporative cooling technology and powered by clean and renewable wind energy. This facility will also be unique because of infrastructure to capture and recycle excess heat generated by our servers to provide heat to the local community. The energy recovered from our servers will be recycled by a newly constructed heat pump facility, supported by 100% renewable energy. This energy will then be directed into the local district heating system, operated by district heating company Fjernvarme Fyn. # The solution This heat recovery project is part of our ongoing commitment to innovation and efficiency, and will support the city’s ambitious goal of phasing out coal by 2025, which is years ahead of Denmark’s national goal to phase out coal by 2030. We worked closely with Fjernvarme Fyn early on, identifying efficiencies in project design from the start. Our proximity to the local heat distribution grid minimizes additional infrastructure and will ultimately enable us to achieve more efficient heat production. While we typically design our servers to minimize the heat they create, in Odense we direct this heated air over water coils, recovering the heat by raising the temperature of the water. This warm water is then delivered to the heat pump facility where the temperature is raised further and delivered to the district heating network and distributed to the local community. # The impact Once completed, our facility’s heat recovery infrastructure will help recover 100,000 MWh of energy per year – enough to warm 6,900 homes. As we continue to make our global operations as sustainable as possible, our team is constantly looking for ways to collaborate with others – developing and sharing solutions that will benefit our communities. The ability to recycle and repurpose heat from our servers is unique to our Odense data center, and we couldn’t have done it without our close partner Fjernvarme Fyn and its district heating network.

**Green Shift in Tissue Manufacturing: Industry Pivots to Sustainable Practices**  

*By Staff Writer*  

In response to growing consumer demand for environmentally responsible products, several leading tissue manufacturers are rolling out innovations aimed at reducing the ecological footprint of facial tissues. From the sourcing of raw materials to the final packaging, companies are rethinking traditional production methods to align with sustainability goals and regulatory pressures.  

**Sustainable Pulp Sourcing**  
Historically, facial tissue production relied heavily on virgin wood pulp harvested from large-scale forestry operations. While such pulp offers desirable softness and strength, it often comes at the cost of deforestation and habitat loss. The new wave of eco-friendly facial tissues draws on alternative sources, such as pulp derived from fast-growing bamboo, agricultural residues like wheat straw, and certified post-consumer recycled paper.  

Suppliers are increasingly turning to Forest Stewardship Council (FSC)–certified timber, ensuring that any wood pulp used originates from responsibly managed forests. Some manufacturers have also entered partnerships with smallholder farmers, purchasing agricultural by-products that would otherwise be discarded or burned, thereby reducing waste and providing supplementary income streams in rural communities.  

**Energy-Efficient Manufacturing Processes**  
Beyond raw material selection, the production phase has been a focal point for environmental innovation. Traditional tissue manufacturing is energy-intensive, particularly in the pulping and drying stages. New technologies are enabling significant reductions in energy consumption. Heat recovery systems capture waste heat from dryers and reuse it in earlier stages of production, while advanced press designs reduce the moisture content of pulp before it enters energy-hungry drying cylinders.  

Several plants have invested in on-site renewable energy generation—solar arrays and biomass boilers powered by production waste are becoming more common. The integration of automated process controls also allows facilities to optimize energy use in real time, cutting down on unnecessary load during low-demand periods.  

**Biodegradable and Compostable Packaging**  
Packaging has emerged as another critical area of focus. Conventional facial tissue boxes often combine paperboard with plastic film, complicating recycling and increasing landfill persistence. In the new eco-friendly lines, manufacturers are experimenting with mono-material packaging made entirely of recyclable paper or plant-based biodegradable films.  

Some brands are piloting compostable wraps derived from polylactic acid (PLA), a bioplastic sourced from corn starch or sugarcane. These wraps break down under industrial composting conditions, offering an end-of-life pathway that avoids conventional waste streams. To ensure durability and shelf life, companies are working with coatings made from natural waxes or water-based dispersions rather than petroleum-derived laminates.  

**Market and Consumer Response**  
Early market data suggests that eco-friendly facial tissues are gaining traction, particularly among younger consumers and those in urban markets with strong environmental awareness. Retailers have responded by dedicating shelf space to these products and promoting them through in-store signage that highlights their sustainability credentials.  

Price remains a consideration, as alternative pulping methods and biodegradable packaging can carry higher production costs. However, some companies are offsetting these expenses through efficiency gains in energy use and waste reduction. The long-term bet is that economies of scale and continued technological improvements will narrow the price gap with conventional products.  

**Regulatory and Certification Trends**  
Governments and industry bodies are adding momentum to the shift. In several regions, single-use plastics in packaging are facing bans or taxes, pushing manufacturers toward compostable or recyclable solutions. Certifications such as FSC, Rainforest Alliance, and Green Seal are becoming powerful marketing tools, influencing purchasing decisions at both the consumer and corporate procurement levels.  

**Future Directions**  
Industry analysts predict that the next frontier will involve digitizing supply chains to track the environmental impact of each production batch from forest or field to retail shelf. Blockchain-based traceability systems could provide consumers with detailed information on sourcing, energy use, and packaging materials via QR codes on product labels.  

Companies are also exploring closed-loop systems where used tissue products and packaging are collected and repurposed into new pulp streams. While technical and logistical challenges remain—particularly around hygiene and contamination—these efforts point toward a more circular model of tissue production.  

As the sector continues to innovate, eco-friendly facial tissues are poised to become more than a niche product. With sustained investment in sustainable pulp sourcing, energy-efficient manufacturing, and biodegradable packaging, the industry is charting a path toward significantly lower environmental impact without sacrificing quality or convenience.

## Abstract This publication presents the results of combined theoretical and experimental research for the potential use of natural clinoptilolite zeolite (CLI) as an odor-adsorbing material. In this study of adsorption capacity, CLI of various granulation was used and its modifications were made by ion exchange using Sn and Fe metals to check whether the presence of metals as potential active centers does not lead to catalytic processes and may lead to enhanced absorption of odorous substances through their adsorption on the created metallic forms. Additionally, in order to increase the specific surface area, modifications were made in the form of hierarchization in an acidic environment using hydrochloric acid to also create the hydrogen form of zeolite and thus also check how the material behaves as an adsorbent. To compare the effect of CLI as a sorption material, synthetic zeolite MFI was also used—as a sodium form and after the introduction of metals (Sn, Fe). The above materials were subjected to adsorption measurements using odorous substances (including acetaldehyde, dimethylamine, pentanoic acid and octanoic acid). Based on the measurements performed, the most advantageous material that traps odorants is a natural material—clinoptilolite. Depending on the faction, its ability varies for different compounds. In the case of acetaldehyde, an effective material is clinoptilolite with a grain size of up to 2 mm. In the case of carboxylic acids, it is material after hierarchization with a fraction of 3–4 mm. In the case of theoretical calculations, information was obtained to show that metallic centers are more stable above oxygen, which is associated with the skeletal aluminum in clinoptilolite. **Keywords:** odors adsorption, ammonia, carboxylic acids, dft, zeolite, clinoptilolite ## 1\. Introduction Zeolites are a group of hydrated aluminosilicates with a microporous structure. They are characterized by a large specific surface area and ion-exchange ability. These materials have been used as membranes, adsorbents, ion exchangers, catalysts or molecular sieves for the treatment of industrial and municipal pollution \ [1\]. Aluminosilicates include zeolites of synthetic and natural origin. Deposits of natural zeolites, including clinoptilolite, are common in many countries such as Greece, Italy, the United Kingdom, Mexico and Turkey. The properties of zeolites in natural materials mimic the properties of many of their synthetic counterparts. Due to their structure, zeolites have many applications, from being used as fillers to molecular sieves and ion exchangers. In recent years, natural zeolites have been studied for their use as catalysts. However, they still require thorough analysis and modification, as they have enormous potential for use on a larger scale \ [2\]. Clinoptilolite minerals suitably modified show selectivity towards cations, anions and can be used as a material for the removal of contaminants. Many studies have been performed on the activation of clinoptilolite by heat treatment or acid treatment, resulting in the elimination of cations from the zeolite structure and pores, obtaining H-zeolite forms and partial degradation of the crystal structure (dealumination). On this basis, two possible modifications of natural zeolite were developed: (i) conversion to the ammonium form of zeolite and heat treatment and (ii) direct ion exchange in dilute acid solution. Activated natural zeolite was used as an adsorbent for the removal of contaminants and was shown to be more effective than activated carbon \ [3, 4\]. In addition, the presence of metals such as Zn and Ag makes it possible to achieve an efficiency of 90% during water purification. In the work of Russo and co-authors \ [5\], an adsorption process using natural zeolite (clinoptilolite) modified with iron was carried out for the removal of BTX compounds (benzene, toluene, xylene) from groundwater. Preliminary studies conducted suggest a promising application of iron-modified clinoptilolite. The combination of adsorption and catalytic oxidation enabled the removal of organic BTX contaminants (15 mg) from a pH-neutral aqueous solution without releasing iron ions from the zeolite structure. The adsorption capacity of clinoptilolite in its activated form during the removal of organic compounds (phenol, chlorophenol) from wastewater was studied. The adsorption rate of aromatic compounds was determined to be fast, and the adsorption equilibrium was reached after 45 min. The adsorption of phenol and chlorophenol was calculated to be 7.977 mg/g for phenol, 9.846 mg/g for o-chlorophenol, 9.981 mg/g for m-chlorophenol and 8.241 mg/g for p-chlorophenol, respectively \ [6\]. Natural zeolite has also been used as an adsorption material to remove the unpleasant odors of ammonia and hydrogen sulfide. For this purpose, first of all, the material was appropriately activated by chemical modification—treatment with acid (HCl 0.4 M for 2 h) and base (NaOH 1 N for 2 h) and thermal treatment (300 °C for 3 h). Subsequently, tests were carried out in which the best material for the adsorption of ammonia and hydrosulfuric acid turned out to be zeolite with a grain diameter of 1–3 mm, activated by thermal treatment \ [7\].

* Locate compost bins and piles away from trees to reduce the likelihood of roots growing into the compost. 
  * Mix materials thoroughly; it's usually not helpful to layer materials. 
  * To speed up the process you can add an extra nitrogen (e.g., cottonseed meal, blood meal) source at each turning. 
  * Keep your compost pile moist (like a wrung-out sponge) but not soggy for efficient decomposition. Excess moisture causes anaerobic decomposition and offensive odors. During dry weather, it may be necessary to add water at weekly intervals. 
  * Do not add branches and other woody materials unless they are chipped into small pieces. 
  * In dry weather, cover the pile to prevent excess moisture loss and to aid decomposition. A tarp or other cover also protects the pile from becoming too wet during periods of heavy rainfall and helps prevent nutrient leaching. 
  * Turn or mix the pile regularly. If fall-gathered leaves make up the bulk of the pile, turn the pile in mid-November before freezing occurs. Do not turn the pile in winter because this allows too much heat to escape and slows decomposition. 
  * When kitchen scraps are collected or composted it can be helpful to mix in a dry, high-carbon material, such as leaves, sawdust, or shredded paper, to reduce odors and facilitate decomposition. 
  * Enclosed compost tumblers can quickly become soppy wet and anaerobic if you add too many kitchen scraps and rotted fruits and vegetables, and not enough brown materials.

**Advancements in Smoke Detector Technology: Moving Beyond Radioactive Components**  

*By Staff Reporter*  

In recent years, the smoke detector industry has undergone a quiet but significant transformation. Driven by both technological innovation and evolving safety standards, manufacturers are increasingly turning to advanced photoelectric sensors that deliver faster, more accurate detection of smoldering fires—without relying on radioactive materials. These developments are reshaping the market and offering households and businesses safer, more environmentally friendly options.  

**The Rise of Photoelectric Sensing**  

Traditional ionization smoke detectors have long dominated the market, prized for their sensitivity to fast-flaming fires. These devices typically use a small amount of Americium-241, a radioactive isotope, to detect smoke particles. While effective, the presence of radioactive material has raised concerns among consumers and regulators alike, prompting calls for alternative technologies.  

Photoelectric detectors operate on a different principle. They use a light source and a sensor positioned at an angle within a detection chamber. When smoke enters the chamber, particles scatter the light, causing it to strike the sensor and trigger the alarm. This method is particularly effective at detecting the larger particles produced by smoldering fires, which can smolder unnoticed for hours before erupting into flames.  

According to fire safety experts, the early warning provided by photoelectric technology can be crucial. Smoldering fires often begin in upholstered furniture, bedding, or electrical wiring, producing toxic smoke long before flames become visible. By responding to these early signs, photoelectric detectors can give occupants valuable time to evacuate or extinguish the source.  

**Technological Improvements and Hybrid Models**  

Recent advancements have enhanced the sensitivity and reliability of photoelectric sensors. Improvements in LED light sources, optical lenses, and signal processing algorithms have reduced false alarms caused by dust, steam, or insects. Some manufacturers have introduced hybrid detectors combining photoelectric sensors with heat detection or carbon monoxide monitoring, offering comprehensive protection in a single unit.  

For consumers concerned about missing the fast-flaming fires that ionization detectors excel at detecting, dual-sensor models are emerging as a popular solution. These devices incorporate both photoelectric and ionization technology, balancing the strengths of each method while reducing the reliance on radioactive materials.  

**Regulatory Shifts and Market Trends**  

Several jurisdictions have begun to recommend or require the installation of photoelectric detectors, particularly in residential settings. Australia’s Queensland state, for example, has mandated interconnected photoelectric alarms in new homes and renovations. In the United States, certain municipalities have launched public awareness campaigns promoting non-radioactive smoke detection options.  

Industry analysts note that consumer preference is playing a significant role in this shift. As awareness grows about the materials used in household devices, buyers are increasingly seeking products that are both effective in fire prevention and aligned with environmental stewardship. Retailers have responded by expanding their offerings of photoelectric and hybrid smoke alarms, often highlighting “no radioactive material” as a selling point.  

**Environmental and Safety Advantages**  

The absence of radioactive isotopes in photoelectric detectors simplifies manufacturing, shipping, and disposal processes. Without the need for specialized handling, these devices can be produced and distributed more efficiently. From a safety perspective, eliminating radioactive components removes potential hazards associated with improper disposal or damage to the detector’s housing.  

Manufacturers also point to the durability of modern photoelectric units. Advances in component design have extended service life, with many models offering ten years of reliable operation before replacement is needed. Longer lifespans not only reduce waste but also ensure consistent protection without frequent maintenance.  

**Looking Ahead**  

The future of smoke detection appears to be leaning heavily toward non-radioactive technologies. As photoelectric sensors continue to improve, and as integrated smart-home systems become more common, consumers can expect devices that are highly responsive, environmentally responsible, and seamlessly connected to broader safety networks.  

Industry leaders predict that within the next decade, the majority of residential and commercial smoke alarms will utilize either photoelectric or multi-sensor designs. This evolution underscores a broader trend in safety equipment: leveraging innovation to enhance protection while reducing potential risks to people and the planet.  

For households considering upgrades, the latest generation of photoelectric detectors offers a compelling combination of performance, reliability, and peace of mind—ensuring that early detection remains a cornerstone of modern fire safety without the need for radioactive materials.

**Wireless Charging for Electric Vehicles Moves Toward Multi-Vehicle Capability**  

*By [Author Name], [Date]*  

In a development that could reshape the way cities support electric mobility, researchers and industry leaders are making significant strides in wireless charging systems capable of serving multiple electric vehicles (EVs) at once. The latest prototypes, unveiled at several transportation technology expos this year, leverage advanced inductive charging pads embedded in parking bays, allowing simultaneous, cable-free charging for vehicles parked within a defined area.  

### From Single-Vehicle Pads to Multi-Vehicle Zones  

Early inductive charging solutions for EVs were designed for one-to-one operation: a dedicated pad aligned beneath a single vehicle’s receiver coil. While effective for private home garages, this model proved less efficient in public or fleet environments where multiple vehicles need charging in overlapping timeframes. The new generation of systems uses a network of synchronized electromagnetic transmitters integrated into the pavement, capable of dynamically detecting and delivering power to multiple vehicles within the coverage zone.  

The key breakthrough lies in adaptive field management. Instead of energizing the entire pad area at full power, the system identifies each vehicle’s coil location and charge requirements, then directs energy in discrete, targeted zones. This not only enables simultaneous charging but also optimizes energy distribution to prevent waste and reduce thermal losses.  

### Efficiency and Energy Management  

One of the main challenges in scaling inductive charging to multi-vehicle setups has been efficiency. Wireless power transfer inherently suffers from conversion losses, but new designs are reporting transfer efficiencies between 90–93%, comparable to some wired fast-charging systems.  

Advanced control algorithms monitor each vehicle’s state of charge and adjust output dynamically. For example, if one EV’s battery approaches full capacity, the system can automatically shift more power to another vehicle, maintaining a balanced load and reducing peak demand on the electrical infrastructure. This load-balancing capability is particularly attractive for urban charging hubs and fleet depots, where energy costs and grid strain are critical considerations.  

### Safety Protocols and Standards  

Safety remains a central concern in the deployment of high-power wireless charging. The latest systems incorporate multiple layers of protection, including foreign object detection to prevent hazards from metallic debris, real-time thermal monitoring, and automatic shut-off if living beings enter the active charging field.  

International standardization efforts are also progressing, with organizations such as SAE International and the IEC working to harmonize guidelines for interoperability between different vehicle makes and charging pad manufacturers. This could accelerate adoption by ensuring that any compatible EV can utilize public inductive charging bays without proprietary limitations.  

### Urban Integration Potential  

Urban planners are taking note of the potential benefits of multi-vehicle inductive charging. By embedding charging pads directly into street parking spaces, taxi stands, or delivery vehicle bays, cities could offer seamless charging without cluttering sidewalks with cables or kiosks.  

In a pilot program in Northern Europe, a municipal transport authority installed a series of inductive pads beneath a stretch of curbside parking. Over a six-month trial, the system successfully served a rotating mix of private EVs, e-buses, and light commercial vehicles, with minimal driver intervention. Vehicles parked as usual, and charging began automatically once the system authenticated them.  

Such integration could dovetail with smart city initiatives, linking charging infrastructure to traffic management systems and renewable energy sources. For instance, surplus solar generation during midday could be routed directly to curbside charging zones, while vehicle charging schedules could be adjusted to avoid grid congestion during peak hours.  

### Market Outlook  

Industry analysts predict that commercial deployment of multi-vehicle inductive charging systems could begin within the next three to five years, particularly in regions with strong EV adoption and supportive regulatory frameworks. While upfront installation costs remain higher than traditional plug-in stations, proponents argue that reduced maintenance, improved user convenience, and the ability to serve multiple vehicles from a single installation will offset expenses over time.  

Manufacturers are also exploring modular designs, allowing cities or private operators to start with small installations and expand coverage as demand grows. This flexibility could make the technology viable for diverse environments, from dense urban centers to corporate campuses and airport parking facilities.  

As the EV market continues to expand, the convergence of inductive charging technology, intelligent energy management, and urban infrastructure planning could mark a pivotal shift in how electric mobility is powered—quietly, efficiently, and without the tangle of cables.

****2] Latent Heat Energy Storage Systems:** ** This type of storage system is
classified as phase change system because they absorb and release thermal
energy during the medium’s change of state/phase. Therefore, the material used
for this storage system is known as phase change materials (PCMs). At first,
heat is absorbed sensibly as input temperature increases but soon it will
reach a point where the heat is absorbed or released at a constant
temperature. A further supply of heat will not increase the temperature of the
material but instead will absorb this heat and this is known as latent heat.
If a PCM has a large latent heat, then better is the material quality. The
point at which heat gets absorbed at constant temperature is usually at the
melting point of these materials. Similarly, as the material solidifies, it
will release the heat to the surroundings which can be harnessed accordingly.
These materials are classified as organic materials such as paraffin,
inorganic materials such as salt hydrates and eutectic materials which are a
mixture of organic and inorganic substances. These materials have high energy
density and take less volume which is why PCMs have been the subject of
interest and research in recent years.
