# Community Solar NREL conducts market analysis, provides technical assistance, and develops tools and resources to accelerate access to community solar. Community solar is a solar energy deployment model that allows customers to buy or lease part of a larger shared solar photovoltaic (PV) system. The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) defines community solar as any solar project or purchasing program, within a geographic area, in which the benefits of a solar project flow to multiple customers such as individuals, businesses, nonprofits, and other groups. In most cases, customers benefit from energy generated by solar panels at an off-site array. Community solar subscribers typically receive a monthly bill credit for electricity generated by their share of the solar PV system, as if the system were located on their premises. Community solar arrangements allow customers to enjoy advantages of solar energy without having to install their own solar energy systems. Community solar projects provide an alternative to rooftop PV systems for customers who: - Have insufficient solar resources or roof conditions to support a rooftop PV system (because of shading, roof size, or other factors) - Do not own their homes or buildings - Are unable or unwilling to install an on-site solar PV system for financial or other reasons. In a 2024 study, NREL estimated the technical potential for community solar in the United States, finding that community solar could theoretically grow to serve all residential electricity customers who are unable to adopt behind-the-meter solar, including low- to moderate-income households. Through this analysis, NREL found that 42% of households and 44% of businesses are unable to access behind-the-meter solar, which is lower than previous estimates. ## Market Status As of December 2024: - Community solar projects are located in 44 states, including the District of Columbia. - Community solar projects represent greater than 10 GW-AC of total installed capacity. - About 75% of the total market is concentrated in the top four states: Florida (3,873 MW-AC), New York (2,110 MW-AC), Massachusetts (1,049 MW-AC), and Minnesota (939 MW-AC). Since 2018, NREL has collected and analyzed data on the community solar market in the U.S. through its Sharing the Sun initiative. Sharing the Sun: Community Solar Deployment and Subscriptions presents U.S. community solar market trends through June 2024. NREL's list of community solar projects, updated through December 2024, provides the most recent details on project sizes and locations. ## State-Level Policies and Programs As of February 2025, 24 states and the District of Columbia have policies that support community solar, 20 (83%) of which include provisions for low- and moderate-income households. !Community Solar Project and Policy Landscape map of the United States indicating states with 1 or more community solar projects, states with community solar enabling legislation, and states with enabling legislation that includes an LMI consideration. NREL tracks and publishes a dataset of statewide community solar policies and the resulting programs that are implemented. The dataset, updated twice a year, collates policies at a state level as well as state-specific program details such as: - Program status (active or inactive/ended) - Provisions for low- and moderate-income households - Capacity limits for programs and individual projects - Subscriber location requirements. NREL also works directly with states through the States Collaborative of the National Community Solar Partnership. The States Collaborative is a group of state-level stakeholders working together to identify and address common barriers to community solar deployment. The collaborative provides members with resources, technical assistance, information, and opportunities for peer exchange. ## Implementation Considerations Other clean energy policies interact with community solar; depending on their design, some projects may have to comply with U.S. Security and Exchange Commission regulations. Net metering is a commonly used mechanism that credits distributed generation owners for the power that their systems contribute to the grid. Community solar participants can be credited through net metering or alternative arrangements such as value of solar tariffs; group billing; or joint ownership. Eligibility depends on utility and state-level requirements. Virtual net metering, also referred to as "remote" net metering, allows customers to receive bill credits for generation from an off-site solar energy system. Some form of virtual net metering must exist for community solar to work properly so that multiple customers can offset their electricity loads from a system located elsewhere. Tax credits, like the federal investment tax credit for solar PV systems, may apply differently to community solar participants, depending on the structure of the community solar program. Variables include whether the participant owns the panels or output (in kilowatt-hours) and if a participant claims an individual or commercial tax credit. There is still uncertainty regarding the exact circumstances in which a community solar participant can claim the investment tax credit.

# Fragrant Tropical Plants for Humid Gardens: Cultivation and Ornamental Use  

Designing a lush garden in a humid climate offers the opportunity to explore an extraordinary range of scented tropical plants. These species not only contribute visually to the landscape but also infuse the air with distinctive fragrances that can transform outdoor spaces into immersive sensory experiences. From broad-leaved ornamentals to delicate flowering shrubs, tropical flora presents a palette of colors, textures, and aromas that thrive in warmth and moisture.  

## Understanding Fragrance Profiles  

The appeal of scented plants in tropical gardens lies in the diversity of their aromatic signatures. Some species release heady floral notes, while others offer citrusy freshness or spicy undertones. For example, ylang-ylang (*Cananga odorata*) is prized for its rich, sweet perfume that becomes more pronounced at night, making it ideal for evening gardens. Conversely, frangipani (*Plumeria spp.*) produces a lighter, creamy fragrance with subtle hints of fruit, perfect for daytime enjoyment.  

Fragrance intensity can vary with temperature, humidity, and time of day. Many tropical plants emit their strongest scent during warm evenings, when volatile compounds disperse more readily in moist air. Gardeners can use this knowledge to position plants near verandas, patios, or pathways where their aroma will be most appreciated during peak hours.  

## Cultivation Considerations in Humid Climates  

Humid regions provide favorable growing conditions for a wide range of tropical ornamentals, but careful site selection and maintenance are key to ensuring healthy growth. Well-draining soil is essential, even in moisture-rich environments, to prevent root rot. Organic matter such as compost or coconut coir can improve aeration while retaining necessary moisture.  

Most scented tropical plants benefit from partial shade, especially during the hottest part of the day, to avoid leaf scorch. Strategic planting beneath taller canopy trees or alongside pergolas can provide the right balance of light and shelter. Regular pruning not only shapes the plants but also encourages fresh growth, which often produces the most aromatic blooms.  

## Notable Scented Species for Ornamental Use  

Several plants stand out for their combination of beauty and fragrance in humid gardens:  

- **Gardenia (*Gardenia jasminoides*)** – Known for its creamy white flowers and intoxicating scent, gardenia thrives in acidic, well-drained soil and partial shade. Its glossy foliage adds year-round appeal.  
- **Michelia (*Magnolia champaca*)** – This tree produces golden-orange blossoms with a sweet, fruity aroma. It is a striking focal point in larger gardens and can be grown near living areas to maximize its fragrance.  
- **Jasminum sambac** – Commonly called Arabian jasmine, this shrub offers clusters of small, intensely scented flowers. It responds well to container planting, which allows for mobility and design flexibility.  
- **Hedychium coronarium** – Also known as white ginger lily, it bears elegant white blooms with a delicate perfume. Its upright growth habit works well as a backdrop in tropical borders.  

## Integrating Fragrance into Landscape Design  

Beyond individual specimens, the arrangement of scented plants can influence the overall atmosphere of a garden. Grouping several fragrant species together creates concentrated scent zones, while interspersing them among non-fragrant foliage plants can provide subtle aromatic surprises along garden paths.  

Layering is an effective design strategy—tall, flowering trees can provide shade for mid-height shrubs, which in turn shelter low-growing herbs or groundcovers. This vertical composition maximizes space and creates microclimates that benefit plant health.  

Water features, such as ponds or fountains, can enhance the experience by carrying aromatic molecules further through evaporating mist. Likewise, raised beds or planters at nose height make it easier for visitors to appreciate delicate scents without bending down.  

## Seasonal Scent Planning  

In tropical climates, many scented plants bloom year-round, but some have distinct flowering seasons. Gardeners can plan for continuous fragrance by combining species with staggered bloom cycles. For instance, pairing the near-constant blossoms of jasmine with the seasonal flushes of frangipani ensures that the garden remains aromatic through different months.  

Night-blooming plants, such as certain varieties of *Cestrum*, can be placed strategically near outdoor seating areas to create a captivating evening ambiance. These species often complement daytime bloomers in a well-rounded sensory garden.  

## Conclusion  

Cultivating scented tropical plants in humid climates is both an aesthetic and sensory endeavor. The interplay of fragrance, form, and foliage can transform a garden into a living tapestry that engages multiple senses. By understanding the unique characteristics of each species—its fragrance profile, blooming habits, and cultivation needs—gardeners can craft landscapes that are as aromatic as they are visually stunning, ensuring that warm, moisture-rich environments are celebrated through beauty and scent year-round.

**The Art of Water Temperature in Tea Brewing: Unlocking Flavor and Aroma**  

When it comes to making an exceptional cup of tea, most enthusiasts focus on the leaves themselves—their origin, grade, and freshness. Yet one of the most critical variables in the brewing process is often overlooked: the temperature of the water. The heat level you choose not only determines how efficiently flavors are extracted from the leaves but also influences the balance between aroma, mouthfeel, and bitterness. Understanding optimal brewing temperatures for different tea types can transform your daily ritual into a refined sensory experience.  

---

### Why Temperature Matters  

Tea leaves contain a complex blend of volatile aromatic compounds, polyphenols, amino acids, and tannins. These compounds dissolve into water at different rates depending on the temperature. Too hot, and you risk extracting excessive tannins, leading to a harsh, astringent cup. Too cool, and you may fail to release the tea’s full aromatic profile, resulting in a flat, underdeveloped flavor. Temperature is therefore a key control point for tailoring your brew to your palate.  

---

### Green Tea: Gentle Heat for Delicate Leaves  

Green teas, such as Japanese sencha or Chinese dragon well (longjing), are minimally oxidized and have a tender leaf structure that is sensitive to high temperatures. Optimal brewing generally falls between 70°C and 80°C. At this range, the amino acids responsible for sweetness and umami are preserved, while bitterness and grassy notes remain balanced. Water hotter than 85°C can quickly scorch the leaves, producing a sharp, unpleasant taste.  

For very delicate varieties like gyokuro, some connoisseurs recommend going even lower—around 60°C—paired with a longer infusion time. This low-temperature steeping can yield an intense, almost broth-like umami experience that is prized in Japanese tea culture.  

---

### Black Tea: Robust Extraction at Higher Temperatures  

Black teas undergo full oxidation, which transforms their chemical profile into one that can withstand—and indeed benefit from—higher brewing temperatures. Assam, Darjeeling, and Ceylon teas typically shine when brewed between 90°C and 100°C. At these temperatures, the rich maltiness, floral high notes, and brisk tannic backbone of black tea are fully expressed.  

For particularly delicate first flush Darjeeling, some brewers prefer to stay closer to 90°C to preserve subtle muscatel aromas. Meanwhile, hearty breakfast blends can take water just off the boil for maximum strength and body.  

---

### Oolong Tea: Navigating the Middle Ground  

Oolong teas are partially oxidized, falling somewhere between green and black teas in both flavor and structure. The optimal water temperature depends on the style—light, floral oolongs from Taiwan often respond well to 80°C–85°C water, which coaxes out their aromatic complexity without overpowering their gentle sweetness.  

In contrast, darker, roasted oolongs like Da Hong Pao can be brewed at 90°C–95°C to fully develop their deep, toasty notes and lingering finish. With oolong, experimentation is key; adjusting temperature across multiple infusions can reveal new layers of flavor from the same leaves.  

---

### Practical Tips for Temperature Control  

1. **Use a variable-temperature kettle**: This allows precise control and eliminates guesswork.  
2. **Cool boiled water for delicate teas**: If you don’t have a programmable kettle, boil water and then let it sit for 2–3 minutes before pouring over green or light oolong teas.  
3. **Consider leaf density and cut**: Finely cut leaves release compounds faster and may require slightly cooler water to avoid over-extraction.  
4. **Adjust for multiple infusions**: For teas that can be steeped several times, slightly increase the temperature with each infusion to maintain flavor intensity.  

---

### Conclusion  

The temperature of your brewing water is more than a technical detail—it’s a creative tool for shaping the character of your tea. By matching the heat level to the oxidation and delicacy of the leaves, you can highlight sweetness, deepen body, or draw out complex aromatics. Whether you’re steeping a grassy sencha, a malty Assam, or a floral oolong, mindful temperature control will help you unlock the full potential of your tea leaves, turning each cup into a deliberate act of craftsmanship.

There are sweet limes and Meyer lemons on the counter near the sink. Makrut limes are perched in the corners of window sills. They’re wonderful to have on hand, make charming housewarming and holiday gifts, and are not hard to make. ## Why I love Citrus Salts Citrus salt is pretty and utilitarian. It provides a pop of surprise flavor to any dish. Friends will love you even more when you hand them little jars to take home after a visit. I tend to use them as finishing salts. Lime salt sprinkled over coconut milk-based curries, or as a finishing touch on spring rolls is a welcome wildcard. Mandarinquat salt sprinkled over homemade sea salt caramels or to top labneh? Give me a minute, I’m adding those ideas to my to-do list. Later in the year, the clementine and Meyer lemon salts are perfect on fava beans and asparagus. And beyond that, on heirloom tomatoes. ## Citrus Salt: Ingredients - **Citrus**: You can make citrus salt from many kinds of citrus. Seek out unusual and offbeat varietals at farmers’ markets in fall and winter. Ideally you want to buy good, organic, citrus. Avoid waxed citrus, but If that's what is available, be sure to give it a good scrub with warm water. Dry completely before zesting. - **Salt**: You'll notice I call for flaky sea salt. For citrus salt, light and flaky salt crystals you can crush between your fingertips work best. I use Maldon, but you can certainly experiment. There are many wonderful salts available. ## How To Make Citrus Salts: Basic Technique I’ll get into more details in the recipe below, but the premise for making citrus salt is quite straightforward. 1 tablespoon of zest to 1/2 cup of salt is a ratio that works well, but you might want to increase or decrease the amount of zest. Again, play around. Make blends. Take notes related to which ones you like, and how you're using them. 1. Zest the citrus. 2. Massage the citrus zest into salt. 3. Bake at a low temperature to dry the salt mixture out. 4. Crush citrus salt in food processor or mortar and pestle if you’d like to change the texture. I like to break it down a bit. It's still light and flaky, just less so. Process them powder fine if you like. A lot of what this comes down to is personal preference. Have fun with this one! And keep an eye out for little vintage, glass salt shakers and jars to store your special citrus salts. ## More Citrus Ideas You'll only use the zest when making citrus salt, but you don't want all that amazing juice to go to waste. The solution? Start by zesting the fruit, then juice it as well. You can freeze the individual juices for later use, or, I like to make riffs on this sort of strong citrus ginger juice. retained in the name for cotton in several Germanic languages, such as German

**Urban Tree Planting Boosts Mental Health in City Neighborhoods**  

*By Staff Reporter*  

**Metropolis, June 14** — A growing body of evidence suggests that tree planting in urban environments is not only reshaping cityscapes but also improving mental health outcomes for residents. Recent initiatives across several major metropolitan regions have shown marked reductions in stress-related illnesses and a measurable uplift in community well-being, underscoring the psychological dividends of greener neighborhoods.  

Over the past decade, city governments from New York to Melbourne have launched ambitious urban forestry programs, targeting streets, parks, and vacant lots. These projects aim to expand canopy coverage, mitigate urban heat, and enhance biodiversity. Yet, beyond environmental goals, public health officials are now championing the mental health benefits tied to these efforts.  

Dr. Alicia Nguyen, a public health researcher at the Urban Wellness Institute, notes that “access to green spaces and tree-lined streets correlates strongly with lower rates of anxiety, depression, and stress-related disorders. The presence of trees within walking distance of one’s home appears to create a buffer against the psychological strains of city living.”  

Municipal data from Chicago’s “Green Mile” project—a program that planted over 10,000 trees along major thoroughfares—reveals a 12% drop in reported stress-related medical visits within neighborhoods that received substantial new plantings. Similar patterns emerged in Toronto’s “Canopy Connect” initiative, where community health clinics observed fewer cases of hypertension and insomnia following the rollout of tree planting campaigns.  

Community feedback has been equally telling. Residents frequently report a heightened sense of calm and improved mood when spending time in shaded, leafy areas. Local parent groups have praised the initiatives for creating more inviting spaces for children to play outdoors, fostering social interaction and reducing screen time.  

Urban planners attribute part of this effect to the visual appeal and sensory experience of trees. The gentle rustle of leaves, seasonal changes in foliage, and the interplay of light and shadow contribute to an environment that encourages relaxation and mindfulness. In densely built areas, these natural elements break up the monotony of concrete and steel, offering psychological relief.  

Economic analyses have also begun to factor in the mental health benefits of urban forestry. Reduced healthcare costs associated with stress-related illnesses, coupled with improved worker productivity in greener districts, suggest a return on investment that extends far beyond the aesthetic and environmental benefits.  

However, experts caution that success depends on thoughtful planning. “Planting the right species in the right locations is critical,” explains landscape architect Jamal Rivera. “Trees must be suited to local climate conditions, soil type, and available space to thrive and deliver long-term benefits. Maintenance, community involvement, and equitable distribution are equally vital to ensure all neighborhoods share in the gains.”  

In Los Angeles, the “Shade for All” program has made equity a central goal, prioritizing tree planting in historically underserved communities where green space is scarce. Preliminary results indicate that these neighborhoods are experiencing both cooler temperatures and improved mental health metrics, narrowing disparities between affluent and lower-income districts.  

As more cities commit to expanding their urban canopy, the connection between greenery and mental health is becoming a powerful driver for policy. While environmental and climate considerations remain important motivators, the immediate and tangible improvements in residents’ daily lives are persuading stakeholders to invest further in tree planting initiatives.  

Urban forestry advocates hope that by framing trees as essential infrastructure for public health, city leaders will continue to allocate resources for planting and maintenance. “When we think of trees as part of our healthcare system,” says Dr. Nguyen, “we begin to see them not just as decoration, but as vital components of a healthy, resilient urban community.”  

With momentum building and positive outcomes mounting, metropolitan areas worldwide may soon find that the path to healthier minds runs beneath the shade of newly planted branches.

**Weaving Synthetic Polymer Cords into Durable Outdoor Furniture: Techniques and Material Insights**  

Outdoor furniture needs to withstand a unique set of environmental stresses: prolonged sun exposure, fluctuating temperatures, humidity, and physical wear from regular use. While natural fibers have long been favored for their aesthetic appeal, modern synthetic polymer cords offer a compelling alternative, especially for projects requiring high durability and minimal maintenance. This post explores practical weaving techniques for synthetic cords, along with an in-depth look at the material properties that make them ideal for outdoor applications.  

---

### Understanding Synthetic Polymer Cords  

Synthetic polymer cords are typically made from polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), or polyvinyl chloride (PVC) blends. These materials are engineered to deliver specific performance characteristics:  

- **Tensile Strength**: The ability to resist stretching or breaking under load. High-modulus PE cords, for example, can support substantial weight without deforming, making them suitable for load-bearing components in chairs or loungers.  

- **UV Resistance**: Prolonged sunlight exposure can degrade many materials, but UV-stabilized polymers incorporate additives that slow down photodegradation. This ensures colorfastness and prevents brittleness over years of outdoor use.  

- **Water Repellence**: Synthetic cords inherently resist water absorption, reducing the risk of mold and mildew. This property also allows furniture to dry quickly after rain, maintaining comfort and appearance.  

---

### Selecting the Right Cord for the Project  

Before weaving begins, consider the cord’s diameter, flexibility, and surface texture. Thicker cords (6–10 mm) provide structural strength, while thinner cords (3–5 mm) are easier to manipulate for intricate patterns. A smooth surface facilitates tight knots and uniform tension, whereas textured cords can enhance grip in seating areas. Always choose cords labeled for outdoor use to ensure they incorporate UV stabilizers and moisture resistance.  

---

### Preparing the Frame  

A sturdy frame is essential for any woven furniture. Common materials include powder-coated steel, treated hardwood, or aluminum tubing. The frame should be designed with anchor points—holes, hooks, or loops—positioned to maintain cord alignment and tension throughout the weave. Ensure that all edges are smooth to prevent abrasion of the cord during installation and use.  

---

### Weaving Techniques  

Several weaving patterns work well with synthetic polymer cords:  

1. **Plain Weave**  
   Alternating over-and-under passes create a simple, uniform surface. This technique is ideal for seat bases and backrests, offering even weight distribution and a clean aesthetic.  

2. **Twining**  
   Two cords are twisted around each other while being woven through the frame. This adds extra strength and a decorative element. Twining is useful for high-stress areas such as armrests or edges.  

3. **Basket Weave**  
   Wider cords are woven in a crisscross pattern, creating a thick, cushioned surface. The larger overlaps improve resilience under heavy use.  

4. **Diamond Lattice**  
   Cords are woven in diagonal patterns, forming diamond shapes. This design provides elasticity and a distinctive visual appeal, often used for lounge chairs or hammock-style seating.  

---

### Achieving Proper Tension  

Maintaining consistent tension is critical. Too loose, and the weave will sag; too tight, and the cord may overstretch or strain the frame. Use temporary clamps or ties to hold sections in place while working, and periodically check the tautness with a tension gauge or by manual inspection.  

---

### Finishing Touches  

After weaving, ends should be secured with heat sealing or specialized polymer adhesives to prevent fraying. For added protection, some artisans apply a clear UV-resistant coating, though high-quality cords may not require it. Inspect the piece regularly for signs of wear—particularly at high-friction points—and replace sections as needed to extend the furniture’s lifespan.  

---

### Care and Maintenance  

Synthetic polymer cord furniture is generally low-maintenance. Routine cleaning with mild soap and water helps preserve appearance. Avoid harsh solvents, which can degrade the cord’s protective additives. During extreme weather events, store pieces under cover to minimize unnecessary stress.  

---

**Conclusion**  
By combining the right materials with well-executed weaving techniques, synthetic polymer cords can be transformed into outdoor furniture that is both stylish and resilient. Attention to tensile strength, UV resistance, and water repellence ensures that the finished product not only looks appealing but also stands up to years of exposure and use. With these considerations in mind, crafters can confidently produce pieces that merge modern performance with timeless craftsmanship.

**Hemp in Ancient Civilizations: Cultural History, Rituals, Art, and Early Medicinal Applications**  

Hemp (*Cannabis sativa* L.) has been intertwined with human societies for millennia, serving purposes far beyond its agricultural utility. Archaeological evidence from Asia and Europe reveals a multifaceted role for hemp in the spiritual, artistic, and medicinal domains of early civilizations. This entry surveys key findings that illuminate hemp’s cultural significance, drawing on excavations, textual records, and material analysis.  

---

**Early Ritual Use in Asia**  
In East Asia, archaeological sites dating to the Neolithic period, such as those of the Yangshao culture in the Yellow River basin (c. 5000–3000 BCE), have yielded hemp seeds and fibers alongside ceremonial pottery. The association of hemp with ritual contexts is inferred from its placement in burial sites and proximity to altars, suggesting its use in offerings or symbolic representations of fertility and renewal. In ancient China, early pharmacopeias like the *Shennong Bencao Jing* (compiled ca. 1st–2nd century CE) mention hemp as a plant with both practical and mystical properties, integrating it into shamanic practices and seasonal rites.  

Evidence from Central Asia, particularly from the Yamnaya and Scythian cultures, indicates that hemp was burned in enclosed spaces, possibly as part of purification rituals or communal ceremonies. Herodotus (5th century BCE) describes Scythians using hemp vapor in funerary contexts, an account corroborated by residue analysis of braziers recovered from kurgan burials in the Altai region.  

---

**Artistic Depictions and Material Culture**  
Hemp’s fibrous qualities made it an important medium in textile production, which in turn held cultural and symbolic value. In prehistoric Japan, the Jōmon people (c. 14,000–300 BCE) wove hemp fibers into cordage and cloth, often decorating pottery with cord-mark patterns that may have had ritual significance. These patterns, impressed with hemp rope, are thought to embody connections between daily life and spiritual beliefs, embedding the plant’s presence in artistic expression.

In Europe, hemp textiles appear in archaeological contexts from the Iron Age onwards, particularly in regions with temperate climates conducive to its cultivation. Analysis of textile fragments from Hallstatt-period salt mines in Austria reveals hemp yarn used in garments and ceremonial wrappings. The durability and distinctive texture of hemp cloth likely contributed to its selection for items meant to endure or symbolize permanence.

---

**Medicinal Applications in Antiquity**  
The medicinal use of hemp is documented in both Asian and European traditions. In China, medical texts from the Han dynasty detail hemp seeds and leaves as remedies for digestive ailments, pain relief, and inflammation. These uses were not merely practical but often integrated into broader cosmological views of health, wherein plants with strong sensory properties were believed to balance elemental forces.

In classical Greece, writers such as Dioscorides and Galen refer to preparations made from hemp seeds, noting their utility in treating earaches and easing childbirth pains. Archaeobotanical evidence from Roman sites, including seed deposits in medical quarters of forts along the Rhine frontier, supports the interpretation that hemp was part of the standard materia medica.

---

**Archaeological Synthesis and Cultural Integration**  
The breadth of hemp’s uses in ancient civilizations underscores its embeddedness in cultural systems. Its presence in ritual paraphernalia, decorative arts, and healing practices illustrates a plant that was not merely a utilitarian crop but a symbolically potent resource. In many societies, hemp bridged the material and spiritual realms, serving as a tangible link between human communities and their cosmologies.

Archaeological synthesis from Asia and Europe reveals patterns of continuity and adaptation: while methods of cultivation and processing varied, the plant’s cultural resonance persisted. This endurance suggests that hemp’s value in ancient contexts was shaped as much by symbolic and experiential associations as by its physical properties.

---

**Conclusion**  
Hemp’s role in ancient civilizations was complex and multifaceted, encompassing ritual, artistic, and medicinal dimensions. Archaeological findings from Neolithic Asia to Iron Age Europe demonstrate that the plant was woven into the fabric of daily and ceremonial life, reflecting its significance in both tangible and intangible cultural heritage. The study of hemp in antiquity continues to illuminate how societies integrated botanical resources into their spiritual and social frameworks, offering a deeper understanding of the interplay between environment, culture, and human innovation.

**Report: Mechanical Pulping and Recycling Processes for Office Paper, Cardboard, and Newsprint**  

---

**Abstract**  
This report examines the operational methods and outcomes of paper recycling facilities with a particular emphasis on mechanical pulping techniques. The discussion encompasses the handling of office paper, cardboard, and newsprint, detailing stages such as material intake, sorting, pulping, ink removal, and conversion into end-use products. Consideration is given to the technological configurations used to optimize fiber recovery, energy efficiency, and quality of recycled outputs, particularly recycled packaging materials.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Paper recycling is a cornerstone of resource conservation and waste reduction strategies in many industrialized economies. Facilities dedicated to this process employ a combination of mechanical and chemical interventions to transform post-consumer paper into usable secondary products. The three major feedstocks—office paper, cardboard, and newsprint—present distinct challenges in terms of fiber composition, contaminant load, and desired end qualities. Mechanical pulping remains a central method for fiber liberation, offering reduced chemical consumption compared to traditional kraft or sulfite pulping, while enabling the retention of fiber length and strength for high-quality recycled materials.

---

**2. Material Intake and Pre-Sorting**  
Incoming paper materials are typically sourced from municipal collection programs, commercial offices, and industrial packaging waste streams. Upon arrival at the facility, loads undergo visual inspection and mechanical sorting. Office paper requires removal of staples, plastic covers, and adhesives. Cardboard is separated according to corrugation grade, while newsprint is isolated to manage ink content. Automated conveyor systems, optical sorters, and manual quality checks ensure that contaminants such as plastics, metals, and non-fiber materials are minimized before pulping.

---

**3. Mechanical Pulping Techniques**  
Mechanical pulping for recycling differs from virgin fiber production in that the input has already undergone one or more manufacturing cycles. The process begins with repulping in large hydropulpers, where water and agitation break down the paper into a slurry. For cardboard, higher energy inputs are required to separate the coarse fibers. Office paper, with its shorter fibers and filler content, is more readily dispersed. Newsprint undergoes gentle pulping to avoid excessive fiber damage.  

Refining stages adjust fiber morphology, enhancing bonding potential for subsequent sheet formation. Disc refiners and conical refiners are employed depending on feedstock characteristics. Temperature control is critical to prevent fiber degradation, and water recirculation systems reduce overall consumption.

---

**4. Ink Removal (Deinking)**  
Ink removal is pivotal for producing high-grade recycled products. Flotation deinking is widely used for office paper and newsprint: air bubbles introduced into the slurry attach to ink particles and carry them to the surface for skimming. Washing deinking, involving dilution and filtration, is more common for cardboard, where ink penetration is less intense but adhesives may be present. Enzymatic pre-treatments and surfactants enhance ink detachment without excessive fiber loss.  

The efficiency of deinking directly affects brightness and cleanliness of the final pulp, influencing suitability for printing papers versus packaging grades.

---

**5. End-Use Product Formation**  
Recovered pulp is blended according to desired specifications. For recycled packaging materials, cardboard fibers are often mixed with office paper pulp to balance strength and surface properties. The slurry is formed into sheets using Fourdrinier or cylinder machines, pressed, and dried. Surface sizing and coating may be applied for certain packaging applications, improving resistance to moisture and scuffing.  

Newsprint-derived pulp, due to its lower brightness and shorter fibers, is commonly directed toward linerboard and medium for corrugated boxes, where visual appearance is less critical.

---

**6. Energy and Water Management**  
Mechanical pulping requires significant electrical energy for refining, though advances in motor efficiency and process control have reduced consumption. Water use is managed through closed-loop systems, where clarified process water is reintroduced into pulping and washing stages. Filtration units and dissolved air flotation systems remove residual inks and fibers from process water before reuse, minimizing discharge volumes and meeting regulatory standards.

---

**7. Quality Control and Market Considerations**  
Quality assurance involves continuous monitoring of fiber length distribution, brightness, contaminant levels, and moisture content. Facilities often adjust blends in response to market demand, such as increased need for lightweight corrugated packaging. End-product specifications must align with converters’ requirements, especially for strength and printability.  

Market fluctuations in recovered paper prices influence feedstock availability; high demand can lead to increased intake of mixed paper, necessitating more intensive sorting and deinking.

---

**Conclusion**  
Paper recycling facilities employing mechanical pulping play a critical role in extending the lifecycle of office paper, cardboard, and newsprint. Through careful sorting, efficient pulping, and targeted deinking, these operations produce a range of recycled packaging materials that meet industry standards while conserving resources. Continued innovation in mechanical refining, ink removal chemistry, and water management will enhance the viability and sustainability of recycled paper products in the global market.

**Report: Advances in Eco-Friendly Beverage Can Packaging**  

---

**Abstract**  
Recent developments in beverage can packaging have centered on reducing environmental impact through innovations in design, materials, and printing technologies. This report examines key strategies in shape optimization, advanced printing methods, and the utilization of lightweight aluminum alloys. The integration of these approaches aims to enhance shipping efficiency, minimize raw material consumption, and maintain product integrity, contributing to more sustainable beverage distribution systems.

---

**1. Introduction**  
As global beverage consumption continues to rise, the environmental footprint associated with packaging has become a critical concern for producers, regulators, and consumers alike [1]. Aluminum cans, long valued for their recyclability and protective qualities, are now undergoing a transformation driven by eco-design principles. Manufacturers are adopting holistic approaches that consider the full lifecycle of the can—from raw material extraction through manufacturing, transportation, and eventual recycling. This report highlights recent advancements in three core areas: shape optimization, printing technology innovations, and lightweight alloy development.

---

**2. Shape Optimization**  
Optimizing the geometry of beverage cans has emerged as a key method for reducing material usage and improving logistical efficiency. Traditional cylindrical shapes are being refined with subtle contour adjustments that allow for:  

- **Material Reduction:** Slight changes in wall curvature and base design can lower the total surface area, thereby reducing aluminum usage without compromising structural integrity.  
- **Stacking and Palletization Efficiency:** Modified profiles enable tighter nesting, increasing the number of units per shipping container and reducing transportation emissions.  
- **Consumer Ergonomics:** Shape adjustments also consider grip comfort and ease of pouring, ensuring user satisfaction while meeting sustainability goals.  

Computational modeling tools, such as finite element analysis (FEA), have been instrumental in simulating stress distribution and optimizing designs before production [2].

---

**3. Printing Methods**  
Printing constitutes a significant stage in the can manufacturing process, influencing both aesthetics and sustainability. Advancements in printing technologies include:  

- **Digital Direct-to-Can Printing:** Eliminates the need for labels and reduces waste associated with label adhesives and paper or plastic substrates.  
- **Low-Solvent Inks:** Adoption of water-based or UV-curable inks minimizes volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions during production.  
- **High-Resolution Imaging:** Improved printing precision allows for smaller, more efficient design elements, further reducing ink usage while maintaining brand visibility.  

These innovations not only enhance the visual appeal of beverage cans but also reduce the environmental load associated with traditional printing methods.

---

**4. Lightweight Aluminum Alloys**  
Material science developments have yielded aluminum alloys with improved strength-to-weight ratios. By incorporating trace elements such as magnesium or manganese, manufacturers can produce thinner can walls while preserving resistance to internal pressure and external mechanical stresses. Benefits include:  

- **Lower Material Input:** Reduced thickness directly decreases the total mass of aluminum required per unit.  
- **Transportation Efficiency:** Lighter cans contribute to reduced fuel consumption during shipping.  
- **Enhanced Recyclability:** Alloys are engineered for compatibility with existing recycling streams, ensuring closed-loop material recovery.  

Ongoing research focuses on balancing alloy composition for optimal performance in both carbonated and non-carbonated beverage applications [3].

---

**5. Integration and Industry Impact**  
The combination of shape optimization, advanced printing, and lightweight alloys represents a systems-level approach to eco-friendly packaging. Beverage producers adopting these innovations report measurable reductions in greenhouse gas emissions and raw material costs. Furthermore, these strategies align with corporate sustainability targets and evolving consumer preferences for environmentally responsible products.  

Adoption is facilitated by collaboration between can manufacturers, material suppliers, and beverage brands, often supported by research partnerships with universities and industry consortia. Regulatory frameworks that incentivize reduced packaging impact further accelerate the integration of these technologies into mainstream production.

---

**6. Conclusion**  
Innovative packaging design for beverage cans is a dynamic area of development with significant potential to reduce environmental impact while maintaining functional and aesthetic qualities. Through shape optimization, advancements in printing methods, and the use of lightweight aluminum alloys, manufacturers can achieve tangible gains in efficiency and sustainability. As these technologies mature, their widespread implementation is likely to become a defining feature of the beverage industry’s commitment to ecological stewardship.

---

[2] Chen, L., et al. (2020). “Finite Element Modeling of Thin-Walled Aluminum Containers.” *Materials Design Review*, 12(4), 215–227.  
[3] Kumar, R., & Davis, M. (2019). *Advances in Aluminum Alloy Development for Packaging Applications*. International Materials Engineering Journal, 27(3), 301–315.

## Abstract **: Salicornia bigelovii Torr. is a potential new crop for coastal and saline lands, because of the oil content of its seeds, its properties as fresh vegetable, forage, and other uses. As a true halophyte, it can grow with seawater irrigation. The aim of this study was to determine the phenology and water requirements of Salicornia as a new plant resource in growing areas for salt-tolerant crops in coastal and saline lands, and elucidate scenarios of sustainability about these issues. Water requirements were estimated in experimental plots on the coastal line and fulfilled with drip irrigation connected to seawater aquaculture discharge ponds, 30 m from the sea. The recorded phenological events were germination, flowering, fructification, maturation, and physiological death. Results reflect the difficulty to adopt it as a new crop because of its long-life cycle, around nine months, contrasting with the life cycle of common crops, from three to four months. Irrigation needs reached a depth of 240 cm, significantly exceeding those of conventional crops. Such limitations are highlighted, but also its potential use as a biofilter of coastal aquaculture effluents, being a productive target-biomass, feasible to be used as a dual-purpose use of water and energy required in aquaculture farms. Keywords: Salicornia; sea asparagus; coastal agro-aquaculture; seawater irrigation; allometric equation ## 1\. Introduction #### 1.1. Water Shortage Limitations for Conventional Agriculture in Arid Zones At present and in the near future, agriculture will need to develop new sustainable schemes to feed future populations. It is clear that water use increases in a parallel rate to total production, and this is going to be a serious problem unless drastic measures are taken \ [1\]. Freshwater limitations in some heavily irrigated regions could necessitate reversion of 20–60 Mha of cropland from irrigated to rainfed management or another source of water \ [2\], as water is a critical resource for farmers, and ensuring access to water is quite important for reducing poverty in rural areas, because poverty reduction will lead to food security \ [3\]. In this context, mankind will have to diversify production schemes, including the integration of livestock, aquaculture, or other, less fresh water-demanding activities; in this context, the proximity of aquaculture to and use of limited high-quality water resources gives a highly site-specific potential for minimizing environmental impact \ [4\]. During the last decades, the use of plant resources of marine or coastal origin is gaining attention, but their use must be sustained on detailed studies, to face the freshwater scarcity and the lack of food \ [5, 6\]. Northwest México is an arid region where freshwater availability for agriculture is drastically decreasing, but on the other hand, it has a long coast sustaining a diversity of biota; the Mexican coastal ecosystems are located in the tropical and subtropical zones between 30° N 116° W and 15° N 90° W, with mild temperatures only on the north, neighboring with the USA border \ [7\]. For the development of this area, regional policies based on the analysis and participatory use of water and natural resources are highly important for a rational planning approach \ [8\]. The above is relevant to mitigate the overexploitation of water in this arid zone, whose main source is groundwater; this issue has become extremely crucial in the last decades, especially in similar arid and semi-arid regions, where the coastal aquifers are particularly at risk due to intrusion of seawater \ [9\]. The shortage of high-quality water is an issue in arid and semi-arid regions. In consequence, the use of water resources of marginal quality is gaining important consideration, particularly in arid regions where large quantities of saline water are used for irrigation. Nevertheless, the use of these kinds of water in irrigated lands requires the control of soil salinity \ [10\]. #### 1.2. The Cultivation of Halophytes as an Option to Reduce the Demand for Fresh Water in Agriculture As an alternative option for coastal development where shortage of freshwater prevails, several species of wild halophyte vegetation are used seasonally for human consumption and grazing \ [11\]. In México, halophytes are distributed along the Pacific Ocean coast and the Gulf of México and grow on saline soils, which are particularly frequent in places close to the coast, as many of them are permanently wet. Under these conditions, true halophyte species are plants that grow in saline environments, with the capacity to develop true tolerance to salts. The importance of the world’s halophyte resources is shown for obtaining fodder, grass forage, and medicinal and oil raw materials, as well as biological agents for reclaiming degraded lands, especially in arid regions, where dire shortages of food are observable \ [12\]. These communities include genera and species with wide distribution \ [13\]. In coastal plant communities in northwestern México, two of the most common plant families are Gramineae and Chenopodiaceae, with several halophytic species \ [14\]. Among the attributes of halophytes, succulence is a common feature in different families, and their tolerance to high osmotic pressure caused by salinity \ [15\]. The annual halophyte Salicornia bigelovii Torr., also known as ‘sea asparagus’ or ‘Salicornia’, of the family Chenopodiaceae, is an annual plant with succulent stems; the whole plant is divided into branches and leaves that are not apparent; groups of plants form compact and frequently extensive colonies. Representative plants reach a height up to 50 cm height, with stems articulated, crass and fleshy, of bright green color; the flowers are inconspicuous and of reduced size \ [16\]. They usually inhabit saline terrains (inland or coastal) such as salt marshes. It is found in flood-prone salt marshes along the northern coast of the Mexican Pacific Ocean, on plains and alkaline coastal plains of the Baja California Peninsula, and on the islands Tiburón and Angel de la Guarda \ [14, 17\]. The differences in growth between halophyte plants as Salicornia and glycophytes such as tomato or lettuce, when subjected to salinity conditions require, for the former, salts for their proper development, while glycophytes reduce their growth and productivity, even with minimum increases in salinity \ [11, 18\]. The promising importance of Salicornia not only lies in the oil content of its seeds, or its potential use as fresh vegetables with high mineral content of their forage, but also because its response to watering, it is suitable candidate as a biofilter to recycle water and nutrients contained in effluents from marine aquaculture \ [19, 20\]. Salicornia has been studied by several researchers, studying its ecology, physiological responses to salinity changes, agricultural management, and utilization \ [18, 20, 21\], also the phenology of related species with an emphasis on floristic aspects, the nutrient content \ [22, 23\], and other issues. On the coast of the Bay of La Paz BCS, México, it is possible to find Salicornia associated to halophytic vegetation and with diversified soil microbiota, both in winter and in spring, which decreases in summer and autumn due to a change in seasonal climate \ [24\]. Even when a productive potential of Salicornia is perceived, taking advantage of seawater from aquaculture effluents and reducing the demand for fresh water required by agriculture, various management-related difficulties in the soil-agroecosystem relationship hinder its adoption. Among other aspects, the duration of the life cycle, the obvious low inclusion in traditional foods, its management at different scales, and the real availability of land compatible with aquaculture are important issues to investigate in greater detail. Accordingly, the purpose of the present study is to corroborate the viability of the halophyte Salicornia bigelovii Torr. as a new crop irrigated with seawater and verify the cultivation period for further adjustments in the design of coastal farms.

# Restoring Outdoor Gear Performance with Durable Water Repellent Coatings  

Outdoor gear—from jackets to backpacks—faces constant exposure to rain, snow, and damp conditions. Over time, even high-quality fabrics lose their natural water-repellent finish due to abrasion, dirt buildup, and repeated washing. This is where durable water repellent (DWR) coatings come in: they restore the fabric’s ability to shed water, keeping you dry and comfortable while extending the life of your gear.  

## Understanding DWR Technology  

Durable water repellents are specialized treatments applied to fabric surfaces to create a hydrophobic layer. This layer causes water droplets to bead up and roll off instead of soaking into the fibers. Many modern DWRs are formulated to bond tightly with synthetic and natural fibers, resisting wear from light abrasion and maintaining performance through multiple uses.  

While the chemistry varies by brand, the principle is the same: the coating reduces surface tension, preventing moisture penetration without significantly affecting breathability. This makes DWR treatments especially useful for technical outdoor apparel, tents, and footwear.  

## Preparing Gear for Application  

For best results, start with clean gear. Dirt, oils, and detergent residues can interfere with the bonding process, so wash the item according to its care label before applying any coating. Use a technical cleaner rather than standard laundry detergents, as these are designed to rinse out completely and avoid leaving residues that repel or block the DWR from adhering.  

Ensure the fabric is fully dry before application. Moisture trapped in fibers can dilute the coating and lead to uneven coverage. If possible, lay the item flat or hang it in a well-ventilated space to dry thoroughly.  

## Applying the Coating  

DWR products come in two main formats: spray-on and wash-in. Spray-on treatments allow precise targeting of high-wear areas such as shoulders, cuffs, and knees, and are ideal for items with multiple fabric types. Wash-in products are mixed into a water bath, saturating the entire garment evenly—convenient for single-fabric items like rain jackets.  

When using spray-on DWR:  

1. **Work in a ventilated area**—ideally outdoors or near an open window.  
2. **Hold the can or sprayer at the recommended distance** (often 6–8 inches) to ensure fine, even mist coverage.  
3. **Apply in overlapping passes** to avoid missed spots.  
4. **Wipe away excess** with a clean cloth to prevent streaks or residue.  

For wash-in products:  

1. **Follow the dilution instructions** carefully to avoid over- or under-treating.  
2. **Agitate the garment gently** in the solution to ensure uniform exposure.  
3. **Rinse lightly if directed**—some formulas are designed to remain without rinsing.  

## Heat Activation for Maximum Performance  

Many DWR coatings benefit from heat activation. After application, tumble dry the garment on low to medium heat (check the care label first) or use a warm iron with a protective cloth. The heat helps bond the coating to the fibers, increasing durability and water resistance.  

If the item cannot be machine dried, hang it in direct sunlight for several hours or use a hair dryer on a low setting, moving continuously to avoid overheating any one area.  

## Maintaining the Treatment  

Even the most robust DWR will wear down over time. To keep your gear performing well:  

- **Clean regularly** with appropriate technical cleaners to prevent dirt from breaking down the coating.  
- **Reapply periodically**, especially after heavy use or multiple washes.  
- **Avoid fabric softeners and strong detergents**, which can strip away the hydrophobic layer.  

## Extending Gear Life Beyond DWR  

While DWR treatments are a powerful tool for moisture protection, combining them with other care practices—such as prompt drying after exposure to rain, storing gear in a cool, dry place, and repairing small tears—will help preserve your investment.  

By following proper preparation, application, and maintenance steps, outdoor enthusiasts can restore and even enhance the performance of their gear, ensuring comfort and protection in challenging conditions. Durable water repellent coatings, when applied thoughtfully, can keep fabrics functioning at their peak for seasons to come.

**Google Expands Renewable Energy Commitments with Landmark Solar and Wind Agreements**  

In a significant move to accelerate its sustainability goals, Google has announced a new series of partnerships with renewable energy providers aimed at powering its global network of data centers entirely with electricity sourced from solar and wind projects. The initiative marks one of the largest corporate renewable energy procurements to date, underscoring the company’s commitment to reducing its carbon footprint and fostering the transition away from fossil fuels.  

**Procurement Agreements and Capacity**  
The agreements, signed with multiple independent power producers across North America and Europe, will collectively deliver over 1.6 gigawatts (GW) of renewable capacity to Google’s operations. This portfolio includes large-scale photovoltaic solar farms in Texas and Nevada, onshore wind installations in Sweden and Finland, and offshore wind projects in the North Sea. Each contract is structured as a long-term power purchase agreement (PPA), securing fixed-rate renewable electricity for periods ranging from 10 to 20 years.  

According to Google’s energy procurement team, the combined annual output of these projects is expected to exceed 4.5 terawatt-hours (TWh), equivalent to the electricity consumption of more than 400,000 European households. The company has stated that this influx of clean energy will match the electricity demands of several of its largest data center campuses, aligning with its goal to operate on 24/7 carbon-free energy by 2030.  

**Integration into Data Center Operations**  
The renewable power will be delivered directly into local grids where Google’s data centers operate, displacing fossil-fuel-generated electricity. In regions where grid infrastructure cannot fully accommodate the intermittent nature of solar and wind energy, Google plans to integrate battery storage systems and advanced energy management software to balance supply and demand. These measures include real-time adjustments to computing workloads, shifting certain operations to periods when renewable output is highest, thereby minimizing reliance on carbon-intensive backup sources.  

Google’s engineering teams are also collaborating with utility partners to pilot “grid-interactive” data centers, which can modulate power consumption in response to grid conditions. This approach not only improves the efficiency of renewable integration but also supports the stability of local energy networks.  

**Environmental Impact and Broader Goals**  
The transition is projected to cut millions of metric tons of CO₂ emissions over the lifetime of the agreements. By replacing electricity generated from coal and natural gas with renewable sources, Google anticipates a reduction in greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to removing more than one million cars from the road annually.  

Beyond the environmental benefits, the initiative is expected to stimulate economic activity in host regions. Construction of the renewable facilities will create thousands of jobs, and ongoing operations will contribute to local tax bases. Google has emphasized that these projects are being developed with strict environmental safeguards, including measures to protect wildlife habitats near wind farms and to minimize land use impacts from solar arrays.  

**Industry Context**  
Corporate investment in renewable energy has surged in recent years, with technology companies leading procurement volumes. Google’s latest agreements build upon its position as the world’s largest corporate buyer of renewable electricity, a title it has held since 2017. The scale of these commitments reflects a growing recognition that data centers—critical to cloud computing and digital services—are major energy consumers and must be powered sustainably to mitigate climate change.  

Experts note that while renewable procurement is a crucial step, achieving 24/7 carbon-free operations requires addressing variability and storage challenges inherent in solar and wind generation. Google’s integration of battery storage and demand-shifting strategies represents a model that other large-scale energy users may adopt in the coming decade.  

**Looking Ahead**  
With these new partnerships, Google moves closer to its 2030 target, setting a precedent for how large enterprises can leverage renewable energy procurement to meet both operational and environmental objectives. The company has indicated that it will continue to explore emerging technologies such as green hydrogen and enhanced geothermal systems to further diversify its clean energy portfolio.  

As the renewable projects come online over the next three years, Google plans to release annual progress reports detailing energy output, emissions reductions, and innovations in grid integration. The company’s leadership has framed the initiative not only as a corporate responsibility but as a catalyst for broader energy sector transformation—demonstrating that the digital economy can be powered sustainably at scale.

**How to Build a Personal Waste Tracking Spreadsheet for Your Household**  

Managing household waste effectively starts with understanding exactly what you produce, how much you dispose of, and where it goes. A personal tracking spreadsheet is a powerful tool for identifying patterns, reducing unnecessary waste, and setting realistic sustainability goals. In this post, we’ll walk through the steps to create a spreadsheet that categorizes different kinds of waste and calculates monthly disposal averages.

---

### Step 1: Define Your Waste Categories

Before you open Excel, Google Sheets, or your preferred program, take time to identify the waste types your household generates. Common categories include:

- **Recyclables** (paper, cardboard, plastics, glass, metals)  
- **Compostables** (food scraps, yard waste)  
- **General Trash** (non-recyclable packaging, broken items)  
- **Hazardous Waste** (batteries, electronics, chemicals)  
- **Special Disposal Items** (large appliances, textiles)  

You can customize these categories based on your local waste collection rules. For example, if your municipality separates glass from other recyclables, create a distinct “Glass Recycling” column. The more accurately you define categories, the easier it becomes to spot reduction opportunities.

---

### Step 2: Set Up Your Spreadsheet Structure

Create a table with rows for each date or week and columns for each waste category. Include the following fields:

- **Date**: When the waste was measured or disposed of.  
- **Quantity**: Measured in kilograms, pounds, or liters — whichever unit is most practical.  
- **Notes**: Optional space to record unusual events (e.g., “spring cleaning” or “holiday party”).  

An example header row might look like:  

| Date       | Recyclables (kg) | Compost (kg) | Trash (kg) | Hazardous (kg) | Notes |
|------------|------------------|--------------|------------|----------------|-------|

---

### Step 3: Gather and Record Data

To populate your spreadsheet, you’ll need a consistent method for measuring waste. This could be:

- Weighing bags or bins before disposal using a household scale.  
- Estimating volume and converting to approximate weight using reference charts.  
- Recording counts for items like batteries or electronics.  

Consistency is key. Choose one measurement method and stick with it so your monthly averages are meaningful.

---

### Step 4: Calculate Monthly Averages

Once you have at least four weeks of data, you can start calculating monthly averages. In your spreadsheet, add a row at the end of each month that uses simple formulas:

- **Average per category**: `=AVERAGE(range)` for each waste type.  
- **Total monthly waste**: `=SUM(range)` across all categories.  

You might also create a summary sheet that pulls monthly totals from each category, allowing you to visualize trends over time.

---

### Step 5: Analyze and Adjust

With monthly averages in hand, look for patterns:

- Are recyclables consistently high? Could you reduce packaging waste?  
- Is compost fluctuating based on seasons?  
- Did a spike in hazardous waste coincide with a home improvement project?  

The spreadsheet becomes more valuable the longer you use it, as you can compare month-to-month and year-to-year data to measure progress.

---

### Step 6: Enhance with Charts and Conditional Formatting

To make your data more actionable, add visual elements:

- **Bar charts** showing category totals per month.  
- **Line graphs** tracking trends over time.  
- **Conditional formatting** to highlight when a category exceeds a set threshold.  

Visual cues help you quickly spot areas where intervention is needed.

---

### Step 7: Set Reduction Goals

Based on your averages, set realistic targets. For example, aim to reduce general trash by 10% over the next quarter or increase composting by 5%. Enter these targets into your spreadsheet and track progress alongside your regular data entries.

---

**Final Thoughts**  

Creating a personal waste tracking spreadsheet isn’t just about recording numbers — it’s about building awareness of what you throw away and empowering yourself to make changes. By categorizing waste, calculating monthly averages, and analyzing trends, you gain a clear picture of your household’s disposal habits. Over time, this simple tool can guide you toward more sustainable living and help you make informed decisions that benefit both your home and the environment.

**Preserving the Elegance: Extending the Shelf Life of Rendered Duck Fat**  

Rendered duck fat is a treasured ingredient in the culinary world, prized for its silky texture, subtle richness, and ability to elevate even the simplest of dishes. Its appeal lies not only in its flavor but also in its versatility—used in roasting, sautéing, baking, and as a finishing touch to gourmet creations. However, without proper care, this delicacy can lose its freshness and aromatic qualities. In this post, we’ll explore the most effective methods for preserving rendered duck fat, ensuring it retains its premium quality for months, and even years, while remaining a centerpiece in fine dining presentations.  

---

### Choosing the Right Storage Vessels  

The first step in extending the shelf life of duck fat is to select an appropriate container. Non-reactive materials such as glass jars, ceramic crocks, or stainless steel tins are ideal, as they prevent any unwanted chemical interactions that could compromise flavor. Airtight seals are essential—oxygen exposure will hasten rancidity. For home use, small glass canning jars with screw-top lids work beautifully, allowing you to portion the fat into manageable quantities so that you only open what you need.  

---

### Refrigeration and Freezing Techniques  

Freshly rendered duck fat should be cooled to room temperature before storage. In the refrigerator, it will stay fresh for up to three months when sealed properly. For longer preservation, freezing is the gold standard. Portioning the fat into ice cube trays or silicone molds allows for quick access to individual servings, reducing waste and preventing repeated thawing and refreezing. Once frozen, transfer the portions to freezer-safe bags, pressing out excess air to further protect against oxidation.  

For professional kitchens, vacuum-sealing portions before freezing offers an additional layer of protection. This method locks in flavor and prevents freezer burn, ensuring the fat remains pristine for refined plating and service.  

---

### Infusing and Flavor Layering  

Incorporating aromatics into rendered duck fat can serve a dual purpose—enhancing its flavor profile and extending its shelf life. Gentle infusions with rosemary, thyme, garlic, or citrus zest can slow the development of off-notes while creating a more complex base for future recipes. Infused duck fat should be strained carefully to remove solids, as residual plant matter can accelerate spoilage.  

These flavored fats are particularly effective in fine dining applications, offering chefs a ready-made seasoning medium for vegetables, grains, or proteins. A rosemary-infused duck fat, for example, can transform roasted root vegetables into a dish worthy of a tasting menu.  

---

### Incorporation into Gourmet Recipes  

Rendered duck fat is a hallmark of luxury in the kitchen, and its thoughtful use can elevate a dish from memorable to extraordinary. Classic French preparations such as pommes sarladaises—potatoes sautéed in duck fat with garlic and parsley—demonstrate its ability to carry both texture and aroma. The fat’s high smoke point makes it ideal for searing delicate proteins like scallops or foie gras, yielding a crisp exterior without overpowering the meat’s natural flavors.  

Duck fat can also be emulsified into sauces, lending body and richness to vinaigrettes or pan reductions. In pastry work, it can replace butter or shortening in savory crusts, producing a flaky but deeply flavorful result that pairs beautifully with game or mushroom fillings.  

---

### Presentation in Fine Dining  

Beyond its role as an ingredient, duck fat can be part of the visual and sensory experience of a dish. A light brushing on grilled bread before service imparts sheen and aroma. A quenelle of whipped duck fat, served alongside charcuterie, invites diners to explore its texture and taste. In plated entrées, a drizzle of warmed, infused duck fat over vegetables or meat just before presentation can create a luxurious finish, enhancing both flavor and mouthfeel.  

For tasting menus, chefs may highlight preserved duck fat as a seasonal or artisanal element, emphasizing its careful preparation and storage. This not only underscores the kitchen’s attention to detail but also educates guests about the ingredient’s heritage and craft.  

---

### Conclusion  

Preserving rendered duck fat is as much an art as it is a science. By selecting the right storage vessels, employing refrigeration and freezing techniques, experimenting with infusions, and incorporating it thoughtfully into recipes, you ensure that this gourmet treasure remains at its peak. In fine dining, where every component tells a story, properly stored duck fat offers both utility and elegance—ready to enrich dishes with its signature depth and refinement, no matter the season.

**Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin)**  

Vitamin B12, also known as cobalamin, is a water-soluble vitamin essential for human health. It plays a critical role in neurological function, red blood cell formation, and DNA synthesis. Unlike many other vitamins, vitamin B12 is synthesized exclusively by certain bacteria and archaea; neither plants nor animals can produce it directly. Humans and other animals obtain it through dietary consumption of animal-derived foods or fortified products and supplements.  

**Historical Discovery**  
The history of vitamin B12 is closely linked to research on pernicious anemia, a once-fatal disease characterized by progressive weakness, pallor, and neurological impairment. In the late 19th century, Thomas Addison had described the condition, but its cause remained unknown. In 1926, George Whipple, George Minot, and William Murphy demonstrated that feeding large amounts of liver to patients could alleviate symptoms, an achievement that earned them the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1934. The liver was later found to contain a specific factor responsible for the therapeutic effect.  

It was not until 1948 that the active compound was isolated in crystalline form by a team led by Karl Folkers in the United States and simultaneously by E. Lester Smith in the United Kingdom. The isolated substance was named vitamin B12. This breakthrough allowed for direct supplementation and ushered in a new era of treatment for pernicious anemia.  

**Chemical Structure**  
Vitamin B12 is unique among vitamins in its complex organometallic structure. At its core lies a cobalt ion, coordinated within a corrin ring—a structure similar to the porphyrin ring found in hemoglobin but with distinct differences in ring contraction. The cobalt ion can form different ligands, giving rise to various forms of the vitamin, including methylcobalamin, adenosylcobalamin, hydroxocobalamin, and cyanocobalamin.  

The elucidation of the vitamin’s structure was a significant achievement in chemical biology. Dorothy Hodgkin determined the complete three-dimensional structure using X-ray crystallography in 1956, a feat that contributed to her Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The intricate arrangement of atoms explains the vitamin’s biochemical versatility and stability in specific environments.  

**Physiological Role**  
Vitamin B12 functions as a coenzyme in two key enzymatic reactions in humans. The first is the conversion of methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, catalyzed by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, a critical step in the metabolism of certain amino acids and fatty acids. The second is the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine, catalyzed by methionine synthase, which is vital for methyl group transfers in DNA and protein synthesis.  

Deficiency in vitamin B12 can lead to megaloblastic anemia, characterized by the production of abnormally large and immature red blood cells, and neurological symptoms such as paresthesia, balance disturbances, and cognitive impairment. Pernicious anemia, a specific form of B12 deficiency, results from autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells, leading to an absence of intrinsic factor—an essential protein for B12 absorption in the ileum.  

**Sources and Absorption**  
Natural dietary sources of vitamin B12 include meat, fish, dairy products, and eggs. The vitamin is bound to proteins in food and released through gastric acid action before binding to intrinsic factor. This complex is then absorbed in the terminal ileum via receptor-mediated endocytosis. In cases of malabsorption—due to gastrointestinal disorders, surgery, or aging—parenteral administration or high-dose oral supplementation can bypass the need for intrinsic factor.  

**Industrial Production**  
Commercial vitamin B12 is produced through microbial fermentation, typically using strains of *Propionibacterium* or *Pseudomonas denitrificans*. The process involves cultivating these microorganisms under controlled conditions, extracting the vitamin from the culture medium, and purifying it for incorporation into supplements and fortified foods. Cyanocobalamin is the most common form in supplements, owing to its stability and ease of manufacturing, though other biologically active forms are also available.  

**Medical Significance**  
The availability of purified vitamin B12 has transformed the prognosis of pernicious anemia from fatal to entirely manageable. It remains a critical nutrient in clinical practice, especially for populations at risk of deficiency, including older adults, individuals with certain gastrointestinal disorders, and those following strict vegetarian or vegan diets.  

From its initial discovery in animal liver to the determination of its complex cobalt-containing structure and the development of industrial-scale production, vitamin B12 has been a cornerstone in the advancement of nutritional science and medicine. Its role in human metabolism underscores the intricate relationships between microbiology, biochemistry, and health.

We all use deodorant to avoid a stinky situation, but all those tubes can present a disposal dilemma. What exactly are deodorant tubes made from? Can I recycle them? Where can I recycle them? And what other options do I have? Earth911 gets to the bottom of these questions and more in our latest recycling mystery. _Feature image: Flickr/ Neil Conway_ _**Editor’s note:** Originally published on September 4, 2012, this article was updated in October 2018._ ## Can I Recycle My Deodorant Tubes? Answer: Yes, at least parts of them. But it’s not always easy. ## How Are Deodorant Tubes Recycled? Why are deodorant tubes difficult to recycle in the first place? In almost all cases, the tubes are entirely composed of plastic. However, it’s not always easy for consumers to determine what kind of plastic their tubes are made from, making it tough to tell if their local recycler accepts the material. ### The Composition of the Tubes Varies Most deodorant tubes are made from high-density polyethylene (HDPE or #2 plastic), low-density polyethylene (LDPE or #4 plastic), or polypropylene (PP or plastic #5), but materials may vary by brand. To make things even more complicated, many brands have a dial on the bottom of the tube that is made from a different plastic polymer than the rest of the container. The cap and protective insert may also be made of different polymers. ### Avoid Recycling Contamination Why does it matter if tube components are made from different plastics? Tossing items that aren’t accepted by your local recycling program into the curbside bin creates recycling contamination, which costs cities big bucks and can ruin an entire load of recycling. To avoid contaminating your local recycling stream, remove parts of the tube that aren’t identified by a recycling code, unless your local recycler tells you otherwise. That includes the dial on the bottom of the tube, the plastic insert that moves the deodorant stick up and down, the cap, and the protective insert that you removed before you started using the product. Product residue inside the tubes can also be problematic for recyclers. Leftover product inside recovered packaging can diminish the value of the material for recycling. Rinse out your tubes with warm water and soap to remove any residual product before you drop them off for recycling. ### The Recycling Process The recycling gurus at TerraCycle, who accept Tom’s of Maine deoderant packaging through their Tom’s of Maine Natural Care Recycling Program, have an interesting way of dealing with the challenges of deodorant tube recycling. “They’re shredded,” Ernie Simpson, lead scientist for TerraCycle, said of the company’s deodorant tube recycling process. “So, the whole step is to take the material, shred it, wash it, melt it and then form new pellets from the original material,” he explained. “It’s the pellets that go into the fabrication of … new items and new applications.”
