### Abstract Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), found in many consumer products, are commonly disposed of in landfills at the end of their service lives. To identify landfill liquids that should be prioritized for treatment, this study aimed to evaluate PFAS levels in different aqueous samples from landfills and identify relationships between PFAS and landfill characteristics. Twenty-six PFAS including 11 perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCAs), 7 perfluoroalkyl sulfonates (PFSAs), and 8 perfluoroalkyl acid precursors (PFAA-precursors) were measured in municipal solid waste (MSW) leachate, construction and demolition debris (CDD) leachate, municipal solid waste incineration (MSWI) ash leachate, gas condensate, stormwater, and groundwater from landfills. Based on the median, results show that PFAS levels in MSW leachate were the highest (10,000 ng L−1), CDD leachate were intermediate (6200 ng L−1), and MSWI ash leachate were the lowest (1300 ng L−1) among the leachates evaluated. PFAS levels in gas condensate (7000 ng L−1) were similar to MSW leachate. PFAS in stormwater and groundwater were low (medians were less than 500 ng L−1). Dominant subgroups included PFCAs and PFAA-precursors in all leachates. PFSAs were also found in CDD leachate, PFAA-precursors in gas condensate, and PFCAs in stormwater and groundwater. Landfill characteristics significantly correlated with included waste proportions (percentage of MSWI ash in landfill, ), operational status (active or not, ) and rainfall (30-d cumulative rainfall, ). The results from this study can be used to prioritize which landfills and which reservoir of liquids (and corresponding subgroup of PFAS) to target for PFAS management. **Keywords:** PFAS, PFAA-Precursors, Landfill leachate, Gas condensate, Stormwater, Groundwater ## 1\. Introduction Landfills are one of the most significant environmental reservoirs of PFAS due to the disposal of PFAS-containing products ( Chen et al., 2020; Favreau et al., 2017; Lang et al., 2016; Schaider et al., 2017; Schultes et al., 2018; US EPA, 2018; Wang et al., 2017) at the end of their service lives. Studies have shown that PFAS can be released from these consumer products to result in high levels of PFAS in landfill leachates ( Benskin et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2022; Hamid et al., 2018; Podder et al., 2021; Solo-Gabriele et al., 2020). These leachates have been shown to impact water quality at wastewater treatment plants (WWTP) ( Masoner et al., 2020) and have a potential to impact natural water bodies. Given that PFAS have been detected in high concentrations in landfill leachates, we hypothesize that other liquid sources like gas condensate, stormwater, and groundwater, may also be impacted by high levels of PFAS originating from disposed consumer products at landfills. To the best of our knowledge, there are no studies that have comprehensively compared all liquid sources (landfill leachates, gas condensate, stormwater, and groundwater) in and across landfills of differing characteristics. In addition, to the best of our knowledge, no studies have been published that evaluate differences among the types of gas condensates in landfills, the influence of stormwater detention systems, nor the correlations between lined systems and groundwater PFAS levels. Significant gaps therefore exist in understanding the PFAS levels in different aqueous reservoirs in landfills. In the growing body of literature related to PFAS in landfill leachates ( Busch et al., 2010; Gallen et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2020, 2022), some studies focused on the performance of onsite treatment systems for their abilities to change the PFAS concentrations in the landfill leachate ( Chen et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022). Also, some landfill characteristics evaluated include landfill size, age of waste, landfill operational status, climate, and geographic location ( Gallen et al., 2016, 2017; Lang et al., 2017; Solo-Gabriele et al., 2020). For example, a study about the relationship between the detected PFAS and operational status of Australian landfills showed that some short-chain PFCAs in active landfills were significantly higher than that in inactive landfills ( Gallen et al., 2016), but this difference was not significant in another study by the same group ( Gallen et al., 2017). Studies that evaluate the impacts of PFAS on groundwater focus on contamination from aqueous film forming foams ( Backe et al., 2013). Only one research group ( Hepburn et al., 2019a, 2019b) evaluated impacts to groundwater from legacy landfills. Given the paucity of comprehensive data focused on different liquid types in landfills, this study aimed to evaluate a wide cross-section of solid waste disposal facilities to identify PFAS levels in leachates (from municipal solid waste (MSW), construction and demolition debris (CDD), municipal solid waste incineration (MSWI) ash), gas condensates (from MSW and CDD gas wells, flare stations, and mixed sources), stormwater (including inlets and outlets from retention areas) and groundwater (from landfills with different leachate containment systems). Results from this study can be used to prioritize which landfills, liquid types within a landfill, and PFAS subgroups should be targeted to minimize off-site impacts. Given the range of landfills evaluated, we also had the opportunity to evaluate characteristics of the landfills that correlated with PFAS levels (e.g., waste proportion, age of waste, operational status of the landfill, and cumulative rainfall) based on statistical correlation analysis. These relationships were evaluated as a first step in understanding operational and environmental conditions which may also influence PFAS levels at landfills. ## 3\. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Detected PFAS in aqueous samples within landfills #### 3.1.1. Comparison of in aqueous samples within landfills Results ( Fig. 1) show that concentration was usually larger than 1,000 ng L−1 in landfill leachates (MSW, CDD, MSWI ash) and gas condensate based on median values. Among three types of landfill leachates, the median concentration was highest for MSW leachate (10,000 ng L−1), followed by CDD leachate (6,200 ng L−1) and the lowest concentration was observed for MSWI ash leachate (1,300 ng L−1). These results are similar to the observation of MSW, CDD and MSWI ash leachates in previous studies ( Solo-Gabriele et al., 2020). Statistical differences were observed between MSW and MSWI ash leachate (p < 0.01); however, leachate from MSW was not statistically different than leachate from CDD (p = 0.19), and leachate from CDD was not statistically different than leachate from MSWI ash (p = 0.65). Although significant differences were not observed between CDD and MSW leachates in the current study, Gallen et al. (2016, 2017) found opposite results; that CDD leachates have higher PFAS levels than MSW leachates. This may be caused by the variability of PFAS levels with the landfill category and the number of PFAS-containing products disposed of in Florida, US (current study) and Australia ( Gallen et al., 2016, 2017) landfills. Specifically, when comparing the sum of nine PFAS evaluated in the Australian landfills ( Gallen et al., 2016, 2017), detected PFAS in MSW leachate from landfills in Australia (~3,500 ng L−1) was similar with that in Florida landfills (~3,300 ng L−1), which is consistent with the similar waste composition (major portion is household waste) disposed in MSW landfills in Florida and Australian landfills. However, for CDD leachates, detected PFAS from Australian landfills (~12,000 ng L−1) ( Gallen et al., 2016, 2017) was higher than that in Florida landfills (~2,400 ng L−1). CDD landfills in Florida accept yard trash, CDD, processed tires, asbestos, carpet, cardboard, paper, glass, plastics, and furniture other than appliances ( Solo-Gabriele et al., 2020); and CDD landfills in Australia accepted CDD, cardboard, glass, paper, concrete, solid metals, timber, and plastics ( Gallen et al., 2017). Yard trash disposed of in Florida landfills may dilute the PFAS concentrations in CDD leachate compared with the Australian landfills. More details about the difference between the Florida and Australian landfills (landfill materials and climate conditions) are provide in the Supplement Table S8. For MSWI ash leachate, PFAS is detected significantly lower than that in MSW leachates, which is consistent with the previous study ( Liu et al., 2022). However, Liu et al. (2022) also showed that detected PFAS in pure ash monofills was 290 ng L−1 which was lower than the median found in the current study. The difference between the current study and the pure ash evaluated by Liu et al. (2022) is likely due to the co-disposal of MSW with MSWI ash in landfill leachates sampled in the current study. The unburned MSW co-disposed of with MSWI ash could preferentially leach PFAS resulting in an increase in concentration. The co-disposed unburned MSW could also explain the lack of statistical differences in levels between MSWI ash and CDD leachates. There was no statistically significant difference (p > 0.18) between the in gas condensate (median of 7,000 ng L−1) and the in any type of landfill leachate in this study. However, a prior study in Canada showed that detected PFAS in condensate was lower than that in landfill leachate from the same site ( Li, 2011). The lack of statistical difference between in leachates (MSW, CDD, MSWI ash) versus gas condensate in the current study may be due to the mixing of gas condensate with leachate in some samples, this mixing would drive the median detected PFAS to be higher than that in pure gas condensate thereby reducing the differences in between gas condensate and leachates evaluated. Evaluating other aqueous samples found within the landfill boundary, stormwater and groundwater, was significantly lower than gas condensate and all landfill leachate types (p < 0.01). Although some comparatively high (>1,000 ng L−1) were detected in 12 out of 77 collected groundwater samples, in the groundwater (collected from landfill with and without lined systems, 140 ng L−1) was statistically lower than that in the stormwater (470 ng L−1, p < 0.01) based on median values.

**Guardians of the Flock: Preserving Heritage Chicken Breeds**  

Across barnyards and homesteads, the gentle cluck of a foraging hen is more than a pastoral soundtrack—it is a living thread in the tapestry of agricultural history. Heritage chicken breeds, with their deep-rooted lineage and diverse traits, are emblematic of a time when poultry was bred for resilience, adaptability, and beauty as much as for production. In an age dominated by industrial hybrids, these breeds stand as vital repositories of genetic diversity and cultural heritage.  

### What Defines a Heritage Breed  

Heritage chickens are generally classified by adherence to standards set by organizations such as the American Poultry Association (APA) or similar bodies worldwide. These birds must be able to mate naturally, possess long productive lifespans, and grow at a slower, more traditional pace compared to modern commercial strains. They are the descendants of flocks that sustained rural communities before industrial agriculture reshaped poultry production.  

### Historical Significance  

In the 19th and early 20th centuries, regional breeds flourished, each adapted to local climates, farming practices, and culinary traditions. The Rhode Island Red, for example, emerged from the New England states as a hardy dual-purpose bird, prized for both meat and eggs. The Dominique, with its barred plumage, is recognized as one of America’s oldest breeds, valued for its calm temperament and dependable egg-laying.  

Beyond their utility, these chickens were woven into cultural identities—appearing in folk art, literature, and even municipal emblems. The survival of these breeds today is a testament to generations of farmers who maintained them despite shifting economic pressures.  

### Distinctive Characteristics  

Heritage breeds exhibit remarkable variety in plumage, comb type, and body conformation. The stately Black Australorp glistens with iridescent green-black feathers and is celebrated for record-setting egg production in the early 20th century. The Speckled Sussex, with its rich mahogany feathers flecked in white, brings both ornamental value and a friendly disposition to the flock.  

Temperament is often a defining feature: some breeds, like the Buff Orpington, are docile and easy to handle, making them ideal for small-scale keepers and families; others, such as the gamey Old English, are spirited and alert, reflecting their historical role in free-ranging environments.  

Egg-laying capacity varies widely. While modern hybrids may outpace them in sheer numbers, heritage hens often lay consistently over a longer span of years, producing eggs with robust shells and rich flavor. Seasonal laying patterns, linked to daylight hours, are common—an echo of natural rhythms largely absent in industrial poultry.  

### The Importance of Preservation  

Preserving heritage chicken breeds safeguards genetic traits that could prove invaluable in facing future challenges, from disease resistance to climate adaptability. Industrial poultry lines are often genetically narrow, making them vulnerable to widespread illness or environmental stress. Heritage birds, with their broader genetic base, offer resilience and adaptability that could help secure food systems in uncertain times.  

Breed preservation also maintains cultural connections. Keeping a flock of Barred Plymouth Rocks or Light Brahmas is not merely an agricultural choice—it is a continuation of traditions that shaped rural life, cuisine, and community identity. Organizations such as The Livestock Conservancy work to document, promote, and protect these breeds, encouraging farmers and enthusiasts to participate in conservation efforts.  

### Engaging with Heritage Breeds Today  

For those drawn to heritage chickens, selecting a breed often begins with understanding its historical role and matching it to local conditions. A cold-hardy breed like the Chantecler, developed in Canada, thrives in northern climates; Mediterranean breeds such as the Leghorn excel in heat and are prolific layers of white eggs.  

Small-scale keepers can contribute to preservation by maintaining pure breeding lines, exchanging stock with other enthusiasts, and sharing knowledge about breed histories. Educational outreach—whether through farm tours, school programs, or local fairs—helps keep these stories alive and inspires new generations to value agricultural biodiversity.  

### Conclusion  

Heritage chicken breeds embody more than aesthetic charm or nostalgic appeal—they are living archives of agricultural ingenuity, regional adaptation, and human-animal partnership. In preserving them, we honor the farmers and communities who shaped our food heritage, and we invest in a resilient future rooted in diversity. Whether through the glossy feathers of a Black Minorca or the calm gaze of a Wyandotte hen, these birds remind us that the past still walks among us, scratching in the soil, calling softly to its keepers.

**Title:**  
Lead-Based Glaze Practices in Ming Dynasty Ceramics: A Historical and Economic Analysis  

**Abstract**  
This study examines the historical use of lead-based glazes in ceramic art during the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), with particular attention to aesthetic trends, economic factors, and the role of transregional trade in shaping glaze composition. Drawing on archaeological findings, historical texts, and chemical analyses of extant artifacts, the paper situates lead usage within broader material culture dynamics. The research highlights the intersection of artisanal innovation, resource availability, and external influences on Ming ceramic production, revealing how glaze technologies reflected both domestic artistic priorities and global trade connections.  

**1. Introduction**  
Ceramics of the Ming dynasty represent a pinnacle of technical sophistication and artistic refinement in premodern China. Among the various technological developments of the period, glaze formulation—particularly the incorporation of lead compounds—played a significant role in determining visual qualities and production methods. Lead-based glazes, which imparted vivid coloration, high gloss, and lower firing temperatures, were not merely technical choices but also responses to market demand, resource distribution, and cultural exchange. This paper explores the historical context for lead use in Ming ceramics and considers how trade routes and economic structures influenced glaze composition.  

**2. Lead in Ming Glaze Technology**  
Lead oxide, when incorporated into silica-based glazes, acts as a flux, lowering the melting point and enabling the creation of bright, opalescent surfaces. In Ming workshops, lead-based glazes were often employed for sancai (“three-color”) wares, decorative tiles, and certain utilitarian vessels. Archaeometric studies indicate that lead content in these glazes could range between 10–40% by weight, depending on intended visual effect and functional requirements [Li, 2008]. The relative abundance of lead ores in certain Chinese provinces, combined with established smelting techniques, facilitated its widespread use in ceramic production.  

**3. Aesthetic Trends and Cultural Preferences**  
Ming artisans pursued a diverse palette, often combining cobalt blues, copper reds, and iron yellows with lead-based glazes to achieve depth and luminosity. The lead-silicate matrix enhanced pigment dispersion, producing richer tones than could be achieved with high-fired stoneware glazes alone. These aesthetic preferences were reinforced by imperial patronage, particularly during the reigns of the Yongle and Xuande emperors, when court workshops produced elaborate decorative wares for ceremonial and diplomatic purposes [Zhang, 2015].  

**4. Economic Context and Production Organization**  
The Ming ceramic industry operated within a complex economic framework that included state-run kilns, private workshops, and regional markets. Lead-based glaze production was cost-effective for certain types of wares, owing to lower firing temperatures and reduced fuel consumption. However, the procurement of lead ores required specialized supply chains. Historical records from the Nanjing and Jingdezhen regions mention coordinated shipments of lead from mining districts in Henan and Yunnan, reflecting organized distribution networks [Chen, 2011]. The economic calculus of glaze formulation was thus intertwined with resource availability and transportation infrastructure.  

**5. Influence of Trade Routes**  
The Ming dynasty’s maritime and overland trade networks, including interactions with Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe, introduced new pigments and glaze technologies to Chinese artisans. While cobalt ore from Persia was a well-documented import, lead sources remained largely domestic; however, foreign aesthetic influences encouraged experimentation with glaze finishes that benefited from lead’s fluxing properties. The Silk Road facilitated the exchange of technical knowledge, including methods for stabilizing lead glazes and achieving specific surface effects. Some scholars argue that the adaptation of certain polychrome techniques in Ming ceramics reflected exposure to Islamic and Mediterranean pottery traditions [Wang, 2017].  

**6. Conclusion**  
Lead-based glazes in Ming ceramics were products of a confluence of local resources, artisanal skill, market demands, and transregional exchange. Their use cannot be understood solely through the lens of technical necessity; rather, it reflects broader patterns of cultural interaction and economic organization. The Ming period’s ceramic legacy demonstrates how material choices were shaped by both practical considerations and the aesthetic ambitions of a society engaged with the wider world.

- Zhang, Q. (2015). *Imperial Patronage and Ceramic Innovation in the Ming Dynasty*. Palace Museum Studies, 18(1), 23–41.

Mineral water is also a very bioavailable source of minerals—meaning the body can absorb large amounts of minerals after someone drinks mineral water. This is significant to bioavailability because the gastrointestinal (GI) tract is better at absorbing minerals in their ionic form.1

Optical Brightening Agents (OBAs) Optical brightening agents (OBAs) are used in graphic papers and tissue to achieve higher levels of brightness than achievable in the wood-derived or deinked pulp and as an alternative to whitening fillers. To a degree there is a trade-off between the level of bleaching in the pulping process and the use of OBAs after bleaching, the latter sometimes being more cost-effective (Moreira Barbosa, Gomes, Colodette, Carvalho, & Manfredi, 2013). Initial stakeholder input raised concerns about the hazardous properties of OBAs in general. Examples of OBAs based on stilbene and tetrasulfonic compounds were mentioned (albeit these were used in laundry detergents and their relevance to the paper sector was unclear). A UNEP SIDS study (OECD, 2005) regarding disodium 4,4'-bis\[(4-anilino-6-morpholino- 1,3,5-triazin-2-yl)- amino-stilbene-2,2'disulphonate (Fluorescent Brightener FWA-1) found no human toxicity concerns but a hazard for the environment (chronic toxicity to daphnia in water). Examination of other SDSs for OBAs found hazards related to eye, skin and respiratory tract irritation as well as aquatic toxicity. Other hazards mentioned were H302 (Acute toxicity category 4, harmful if swallowed) and H314 (Skin corrosion Category 1B, causes burns). However, it was pointed out that these last two hazards are not specifically restricted by the horizontal EU Ecolabel criteria. Blue Angel bans the use of OBAs entirely in some papers (essentially where brightness is not deemed essential) but allows the use of low hazard OBAs in ‘white’ papers: “The use of optical brighteners shall not be permitted. Notwithstanding this, SC, LWC, MWC and HWC papers (according to Appendix 1 to these Basic Award Criteria) may be produced using the optical brighteners C.I.220, benzenesulfonic acid, 2,2'-(1,2-ethendiyl) bis \[5\[4-\[bis(2-hydroxy- ethyl) amnino\]-6-\[(4-sulfophenyl)amino\]- 1,3,5, triazin-2yl\]amino\]-, tetra sodium salt and C.I. 113 or C.I.28 disodium salt 4,4'-bis\[6-anilino-4-\[bis(2-hxdroethyl)amino\]-1,3,5-triazin-2- yl\]amino\]stilbene-2,2'-disulphonate.” The Green Seal standard restricts OBAs in the following manner: "Optical brighteners may be used as a functional papermaking additive at a dosage not to exceed 200 parts per million (0.02%) by weight in the finished product. This level does not include any optical brighteners that may be present in the furnish through the use of recovered materials." However, feedback received from the European paper industry revealed that there are REACH registered OBAs available on the market that exhibit none of the restricted CLP hazards mentioned in criterion 4b). Any OBAs that do possess restricted CLP hazards should quite rightly be excluded from use in any EU Ecolabel paper product if resulting in their presence in levels exceeding 0.1% (w/w). Consequently it was decided that the horizontal criterion 4b) was sufficiently restrictive and no stand-alone criterion was required for OBAs. This approach restricts the use of OBAs based on substances with any of a large number of hazards but at the same time allows producers to decide on how best to achieve the target brightness of their paper product (i.e. more bleaching or use more non-hazardous/less hazardous OBA). The overly prescriptive approach of the Blue Angel was criticised and it was questioned if the Green Seal requirement does not simply result in a shifting of the life cycle impact from savings on impacts related to OBA to increases in impacts due to extra bleaching.

There is a growing interest in the utilization of waste biomass products in construction materials to enhance the physical properties of conventional concrete for effective waste management practices and to reduce the carbon footprint of the cement used. Primarily, the waste biomass residues were directly incinerated in open fields to avoid the handling cost or landfill which produces methane gas a more potent greenhouse gas. Certain natural fibers like bamboo, flax, cotton, hemp, jute, hardwood or softwood are a strong natural fiber source[39], [40], [41], [42], [43] and bio-based additives like cellulose nanocrystals[44], [45], [46]lignin[31], [47] that is readily available and cheap source to develop reinforced concrete. However, preprocessing is required to directly use those fibers into concrete matrix and that adds more cost to the process. Moreover, the hydrophilic properties of natural fibers adversely affect the durability (especially water absorption) of the resultant fiber reinforced concrete composite. As a solution, these organic waste materials can be pyrolyzed to biochar, which is a carbon rich highly porous solid material derived from thermochemical conversion of lignocellulosic biomass in the limited/controlled oxygen environment in the temperature range of 450-5500 C[48]. Until this decade, biochar was mainly used as a soil amending or conditioning agent to reduce soil acidity, nutrient leaching, emission of greenhouse gases, fertilizer, and irrigation requirement, and to improve water quality, but now biochar finds its applications in cosmetics, carbon storage, textiles, wastewater treatment, catalysis, polymer composites, and construction materials[49], [50]. A very limited study has been carried out to investigate biochar in construction material and carbon sequestration point of view. The highly porous structure and water holding capacity of biochar can be positively used as a “water-pockets” for uniform and timely curing of concrete. The released water can be used for boosting the cement hydration reaction to produce more hydrated products which give ultimate strength to the concrete composites[31]. Moreover, finely pulverized biochar also provides filling effects to reduce the overall porosity to form more dense structure and positively influence its final strength. Biochar also offers advantageous characteristics in reducing the total cement quantity used and subsequently lowers the carbon footprints developed by the production of cement. However, several factors significantly impact the yield, specific surface area, pore volume, and other microstructural properties of the biochar obtained. For instance, biochar produced at low temperature (< 500ºC) is most likely to retain its pristine nutrients and organic matter from the source biomass and offers higher biochar yield with less energy-intensive input[51]. These nutrients (Si, and Ca-based compounds) could be helpful to alter the course of the hydration kinetics of the clinker phases[52]. The lower temperature pyrolysis produces more micropores compared to the higher temperature pyrolysis could be advantageous to reduce the overall porosity of concrete by providing filling[53]. Hence, the biomass pyrolyzing conditions should be meticulously considered to obtain desired biochar properties.

**Nutritional Differences Between Organic and Conventional Palm Oil: Fatty Acid Composition, Vitamin E Content, and Implications for Human Health**  

---

**Abstract**  
Palm oil is one of the most widely consumed vegetable oils globally, used extensively in culinary applications due to its high oxidative stability and neutral flavor profile. While environmental and sustainability considerations have been the subject of separate research, the present study focuses on the nutritional distinctions between organic and conventional palm oil, particularly with respect to fatty acid composition, vitamin E (tocopherols and tocotrienols) content, and potential impacts on human health. Data from recent analyses indicate that differences in cultivation practices may influence micronutrient retention and sensory characteristics, with implications for dietary quality and cooking performance.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Palm oil (Elaeis guineensis) is extracted from the mesocarp of the fruit of the oil palm and is characterized by a high proportion of saturated and monounsaturated fatty acids, along with notable levels of vitamin E compounds [1]. Organic palm oil is produced under agricultural systems that exclude synthetic pesticides and fertilizers, adhering to standards such as those set by the European Union Organic Certification framework. Conventional palm oil, by contrast, is typically cultivated using synthetic inputs designed to maximize yield and manage pests. While both types undergo similar post-harvest processing, differences in agronomic practices may influence the chemical composition of the oil. This paper examines the available evidence on compositional variability and its potential health implications.

---

**2. Fatty Acid Composition**  
Palm oil’s lipid profile is dominated by palmitic acid (~44–45%), oleic acid (~39–40%), and linoleic acid (~10%). Comparative studies between organic and conventional samples have found only minor variations in the relative percentages of these fatty acids [2]. In some analyses, organic palm oil exhibited slightly higher oleic acid content, potentially attributable to differences in soil management and cultivar selection [3]. Saturated fat levels remained largely comparable across production systems, suggesting that the impact of organic cultivation on macro-level lipid composition is limited.  

The stability of fatty acid composition is important for culinary uses, as palm oil’s high saturation confers resistance to oxidative degradation during frying and baking. Even small variations in unsaturated fatty acid content can influence oxidative stability and shelf life, though these differences are generally within the range of natural variability observed across geographic regions.

---

**3. Vitamin E Content**  
Vitamin E in palm oil is present as both tocopherols and tocotrienols, compounds with antioxidant properties and potential neuroprotective effects [4]. Organic palm oil samples have been reported to retain marginally higher concentrations of total vitamin E compared to conventional counterparts, possibly due to lower exposure to synthetic agrochemicals and reduced oxidative stress during fruit development [5].  

In particular, tocotrienol levels—associated with benefits in lipid metabolism and neurodegenerative disease prevention—were found to be elevated in some organic samples. However, post-harvest handling, refining processes, and storage conditions exert a more pronounced influence on vitamin E retention than cultivation method alone. Cold-pressed and minimally refined palm oils, whether organic or conventional, generally exhibit the highest antioxidant content.

---

**4. Impact on Human Health**  
From a nutritional standpoint, both organic and conventional palm oils share a similar profile in terms of caloric density and primary fatty acid composition. The modest differences in micronutrient content, especially vitamin E, could confer incremental health benefits in organic variants, though these effects require further clinical substantiation [6].  

Palm oil’s saturated fat content has been linked to elevated LDL cholesterol in some populations, yet its balanced monounsaturated fraction and antioxidant compounds may mitigate certain cardiovascular risks when consumed in moderation and within a balanced diet. Organic palm oil’s slightly higher antioxidant potential could marginally enhance its health profile, but dietary context remains the predominant determinant of health outcomes.

---

**5. Culinary Uses and Taste Profiles**  
In culinary applications, palm oil’s semi-solid consistency at room temperature and high smoke point make it suitable for frying, baking, and as a shortening substitute. Organic palm oil often retains a more pronounced natural aroma and deeper golden-orange hue, attributed to higher carotenoid content prior to refining [7]. These sensory attributes can influence consumer preference, particularly in applications where flavor and color are desirable, such as artisanal baked goods or traditional dishes. Conventional refined palm oil tends to have a more neutral flavor, making it versatile for products requiring minimal sensory interference.

---

**6. Conclusion**  
Organic and conventional palm oils are nutritionally similar in macrocomposition, with organic variants showing minor increases in certain micronutrients, particularly tocotrienols. While these differences may enhance antioxidant intake marginally, the overall health impact is contingent on consumption patterns, refinement level, and integration within a balanced diet. Culinary performance remains strong in both types, with organic palm oil potentially offering enhanced sensory qualities in minimally processed forms.

---

**Title:**  
Biomechanical and Cardiovascular Adaptations to Prolonged Daily Cycling: Implications for Performance and Health

**Abstract**  
Cycling is a mechanically efficient mode of human-powered locomotion, offering substantial cardiovascular and musculoskeletal benefits when performed regularly. This paper examines the biomechanical processes underlying cycling efficiency, the cardiovascular adaptations associated with prolonged daily training, and the implications for endurance performance. Optimal regimens for athletes and recreational riders are discussed, along with nutritional strategies that support sustained exercise. Evidence from longitudinal studies and controlled trials is integrated to provide a comprehensive understanding of how daily cycling influences muscle fiber composition, cardiac output, and metabolic resilience.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Cycling has long been recognized as a low-impact, high-yield form of aerobic exercise. Its efficiency derives from the continuous, cyclical engagement of large muscle groups in the lower limbs, coupled with mechanical leverage through the crank system [1]. When performed daily over extended durations, cycling induces both central and peripheral adaptations that enhance endurance capacity. Understanding these adaptations is essential for designing training programs that maximize health benefits while minimizing injury risk.

---

**2. Biomechanical Considerations**  
The biomechanics of cycling involve coordinated activation of the quadriceps, hamstrings, gluteal muscles, and calf musculature. Pedal stroke mechanics can be divided into the power phase (downstroke) and recovery phase (upstroke), with optimal force application occurring between 90° and 180° of crank rotation [2]. Prolonged daily cycling promotes neuromuscular efficiency, characterized by reduced co-contraction of antagonistic muscles and improved force symmetry between limbs. Over time, these changes can lead to increased gross efficiency, defined as the ratio of mechanical work output to metabolic energy input.

Muscle fiber adaptation is a key outcome of sustained cycling. Type IIa fibers, which possess both oxidative and glycolytic capacities, tend to shift toward a more oxidative profile under endurance conditions [3]. This enhances fatigue resistance and promotes sustained power generation at submaximal intensities.

---

**3. Cardiovascular Adaptations**  
Daily cycling imposes a consistent aerobic load, stimulating central cardiovascular adaptations such as increased stroke volume, reduced resting heart rate, and improved cardiac efficiency [4]. Peripheral adaptations include increased capillary density in working muscles, facilitating enhanced oxygen delivery and waste removal. These changes collectively raise maximal oxygen uptake (VO₂max), a primary determinant of endurance performance.

Prolonged cycling also influences autonomic balance, with regular training shifting the sympathovagal balance toward parasympathetic dominance at rest, indicative of improved recovery capacity [5]. Such adaptations contribute not only to athletic performance but also to long-term cardiovascular health, reducing risk factors associated with heart disease and metabolic syndrome.

---

**4. Training Regimens for Sustained Performance**  
Optimal daily cycling programs must balance intensity, volume, and recovery to avoid overtraining. For athletes, polarized training models—combining high-intensity intervals with low-intensity endurance rides—have been shown to yield superior adaptations compared to uniform moderate-intensity training [6]. Recreational riders may benefit from moderate-intensity continuous training, which is more sustainable and aligns with health-oriented goals.

Progressive overload remains a central principle: gradually increasing duration or resistance ensures continued physiological adaptation. Monitoring heart rate variability and perceived exertion can guide adjustments to training load, preventing chronic fatigue.

---

**5. Nutritional Strategies for Endurance Cycling**  
Sustained daily cycling requires adequate nutritional support to maintain energy balance and facilitate recovery. Carbohydrate intake is critical for replenishing muscle glycogen, particularly when training volumes exceed 90 minutes per day. Protein consumption of 1.2–1.6 g·kg⁻¹·day⁻¹ supports muscle repair and adaptation [7]. Hydration strategies must account for fluid losses through sweat, with electrolyte replacement necessary during prolonged sessions in warm environments.

Micronutrients such as iron and vitamin D play supportive roles in oxygen transport and muscle function, respectively. Periodized nutrition—altering macronutrient ratios in accordance with training phases—can further enhance training responsiveness.

---

**6. Conclusion**  
Prolonged daily cycling elicits a wide range of biomechanical and cardiovascular adaptations that enhance endurance performance and promote overall health. These benefits are maximized when training programs are tailored to individual capacity, with careful attention to intensity distribution, recovery, and nutritional support. Continued research into the interplay between biomechanics, cardiovascular function, and metabolism will refine our understanding of optimal cycling practices for diverse populations.

---

**References**

**Report: Environmental Impact of Aluminum Beverage Cans and Strategies for Carbon Footprint Reduction**  

---

**Abstract**  
Aluminum beverage cans represent a significant portion of global packaging consumption. While aluminum is highly recyclable, its production involves energy-intensive processes that contribute to greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. This report examines the environmental impacts associated with the manufacturing and transportation of aluminum cans, identifies key sources of emissions, and evaluates strategies for reducing their carbon footprint through energy-efficient smelting technologies and improved recycling infrastructure.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
Aluminum cans are widely used for beverages due to their durability, light weight, and resistance to corrosion. The material’s recyclability has been promoted as a major environmental advantage, with recycling rates for aluminum exceeding those of many other packaging materials. However, the primary production of aluminum from bauxite ore remains one of the most energy-demanding industrial processes, emitting significant quantities of carbon dioxide and other GHGs. Understanding the lifecycle impacts of aluminum beverage cans is essential for designing effective mitigation strategies.  

---

**2. Greenhouse Gas Emissions in Aluminum Can Production**  

**2.1 Primary Production**  
The production process begins with mining bauxite ore, which is refined into alumina via the Bayer process. Alumina is then reduced to aluminum metal through electrolytic smelting, typically using the Hall–Héroult process. This stage is particularly energy-intensive, relying heavily on electricity, which in many regions is generated from fossil fuels. Estimates indicate that primary aluminum production emits approximately 10–12 kg CO₂-equivalent per kilogram of aluminum produced [1].  

**2.2 Transportation Impacts**  
Once manufactured, aluminum coils and sheets are transported to can-making facilities, and finished cans are distributed to beverage producers and ultimately to retail outlets. While aluminum’s light weight reduces transport emissions relative to heavier packaging materials, the global nature of supply chains often entails long-distance shipping, contributing additional GHG emissions.  

---

**3. Recycling as a Mitigation Strategy**  

**3.1 Energy Savings from Recycling**  
Recycling aluminum requires only about 5% of the energy needed for primary production, resulting in substantial reductions in GHG emissions. Secondary aluminum production emits roughly 0.5 kg CO₂-equivalent per kilogram of metal, making it a critical component of sustainable packaging strategies.  

**3.2 Current Recycling Infrastructure**  
Although aluminum recycling rates are high in certain regions, collection systems vary widely. Inconsistent infrastructure and contamination in recycling streams can reduce efficiency and increase energy requirements for reprocessing. Improved sorting technologies, public education campaigns, and standardized collection protocols are necessary to maximize recovery rates.  

---

**4. Energy-Efficient Smelting Technologies**  

**4.1 Inert Anode Technology**  
Emerging smelting methods, such as inert anode electrolytic cells, have the potential to eliminate direct carbon emissions from the smelting process by replacing carbon-based anodes with non-consumable materials. Pilot projects indicate significant GHG reductions when coupled with renewable electricity sources.  

**4.2 Renewable Energy Integration**  
Transitioning smelting operations to renewable electricity sources—such as hydropower, wind, or solar—can drastically cut the carbon intensity of primary aluminum production. Several smelters in regions with abundant renewable resources have demonstrated the feasibility of this approach.  

---

**5. Policy and Industry Actions**  

**5.1 Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)**  
Policies that place responsibility for end-of-life management on producers can incentivize design for recyclability and investment in recycling infrastructure. EPR frameworks have been adopted in various jurisdictions to ensure that beverage packaging is collected and recycled efficiently.  

**5.2 Industry Collaboration**  
Cross-sector collaboration among mining companies, smelters, can manufacturers, beverage brands, and waste management firms is vital for implementing low-carbon technologies and harmonizing recycling systems.  

---

**6. Conclusion**  
Aluminum beverage cans offer clear advantages in terms of recyclability and material strength, yet their environmental impact is closely tied to the energy-intensive nature of primary aluminum production and the efficiency of recycling systems. Reducing the carbon footprint of aluminum cans requires a multifaceted approach: advancing energy-efficient smelting technologies, expanding and improving recycling infrastructure, and integrating renewable energy into production processes. Coordinated efforts among policymakers, industry stakeholders, and consumers can help achieve significant GHG reductions, ensuring aluminum packaging remains a viable and sustainable choice for beverage distribution.  

---

**References**  
[1] International Aluminium Institute. *Global Aluminium Cycle Report*, 2022.  
[2] U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. *Greenhouse Gas Emissions from the Aluminum Industry*, 2021.  
[3] European Commission. *Circular Economy and Aluminum Packaging*, 2020.

  * **Specific challenges in 2022 contributed to the growth in emissions.** Of the 321 Mt CO  2  increase, 60 Mt CO  2  can be attributed to cooling and heating demand in extreme weather and another 55 Mt CO  2  to nuclear power plants being offline. 
  * **CO** **2** **growth in 2022 was well below global GDP growth of 3.2%** , reverting to a decade-long trend of decoupling emissions and economic growth that was broken by 2021’s sharp rebound in emissions. Improvements in the CO  2  intensity of energy use were slightly slower than the past decade’s average. 
  * **Emissions from natural gas fell by 1.6% or 118 Mt** , following continued tightening of supply exacerbated by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Reductions in emissions from gas were particularly pronounced in Europe (-13.5%). The Asia Pacific region also saw unprecedented reductions (-1.8%). 
  * **Increased emissions from coal** **more than offset reductions from natural gas** . Amid a wave of gas-to-coal switching during the global energy crisis, CO  2  emissions from coal grew by 1.6% or 243 Mt, far exceeding the last decade’s average growth rate, and reaching a new all-time high of almost 15.5 Gt. 
  * **Emissions from oil grew even more than emissions from coal, rising by 2.5% or 268 Mt to 11.2 Gt.** Around half of the increase came from aviation, as air travel continued to rebound from pandemic lows, nearing 80% of 2019 levels. Tempering this increase, electric vehicles continued to gain momentum in 2022, with over 10 million cars sold, exceeding 14% of global car sales. 
  * **The biggest sectoral increase in emissions in 2022 came from electricity and heat generation,** whose emissions were up by 1.8% or 261 Mt. In particular, global emissions from coal-fired electricity and heat generation grew by 224 Mt or 2.1%, led by emerging economies in Asia. 
  * **A strong expansion of renewables** **limited the rebound in coal power emissions** . Renewables met 90% of last year’s global growth in electricity generation. Solar PV and wind generation each increased by around 275 TWh, a new annual record. 
  * **Emissions from industry declined by 1.7% to 9.2 Gt** **** **last year** . While several regions saw manufacturing curtailments, the global decline was largely driven by a 161 Mt CO  2  decrease in China’s industry emissions, reflecting a 10% decline in cement production and a 2% decline in steel making. 
  * **China’s emissions were relatively flat in 2022, declining by 23 Mt or 0.2%.** Growing emissions from combustion were offset by declines from industrial processes. Weaker economic growth, declining construction activity, and strict Covid-19 measures led to reductions in industrial and transport emissions. Power sector emissions growth slowed compared with the average of the past decade but still reached 2.6%. 
  * **The European Union saw a 2.5% or 70 Mt reduction in CO** **2** **emissions** despite oil and gas market disruptions, hydro shortfalls due to drought, and numerous nuclear plants going offline. **** Buildings sector emissions fell markedly, helped by a mild winter. Although power sector emissions increased by 3.4%, coal use was not as high as anticipated. For the first time, electricity generation from wind and solar PV combined exceeded that of gas or nuclear. 
  * **US emissions grew by 0.8% or 36 Mt. The buildings sector saw the highest emissions growth, driven by extreme temperatures.** The main emissions reductions came from electricity and heat generation, thanks to unprecedented increases in solar PV and wind, as well as coal-to-gas switching. While many other countries reduced their natural gas use, the United States saw an increase of 89 Mt in CO  2  emissions from gas, as it was called upon to meet peak electricity demand during summer heat waves.

of zones, debating where the imaginary lines between them are drawn. Zoning is

energy and maintenance requirements. This is all. The zones themselves are
arbitrary and imagine and there are no ‘lines’ in the landscape that determine

close to the kitchen and makes much more sense as our ‘zone 1’ because it fits

as a NOx adsorption catalyst system or a urea/ammonia selective catalytic reduction system, for
control of NOx emissions.
Gasoline powered engines have used an electric spark to ignite a fuel and air mixture to
produce power since their invention. A fuel and air mixture is drawn into an engine cylinder and
ignited at a defined, precise moment releasing energy as a controlled explosion.927
 The energy
released during this explosion is translated to the engine crankshaft and then out of the engine to
perform whatever work the engine is tasked to do.

****2] Solar Distillation and Desalination:** ** Another application for solar
thermal systems is for water purification through solar distillation and
desalination. Distillation is one of the oldest methods that are commonly used
to purify a substance by filtering out the components based on their
volatilities. It involves evaporating a solvent in one location and condensing
the solvent vapour in another location. This purifies the solvent and when the
energy supplied to facilitate this process is provided by solar radiation, it
is termed as solar distillation. Conventionally, distillation occurs in
constant conditions of temperature, pressure and flow rate but solar
distillation is dependent on the solar insolation available with the highest
performance shown during maximum irradiance. It also varies throughout the
year with it showing better performance during the warmer months as compared
to the colder months. The major advantages of opting for solar distillation
are because the need for regular operation and maintenance is minimized due to
the absence of moving parts. The use of solar radiation also completely avoids
burning of fossil fuels and hence has zero greenhouse gas semissions. The
versatility in being able to install these systems in remote locations also
provides an added advantage. Water desalination using solar thermal energy is
a classification of solar distillation which uses passive systems to minimize
dependency on construction, operation and maintenance. Using a solar collector
significantly reduced thermal losses and increased efficiency because of the
small surface area of the absorber and because of the lack of need for extra
components.

In drinking water, the concentration of chlorine is usually very low and is
thus not a concern in acute exposure. More of a concern is the long term risk
of cancer due to chronic exposure to chlorinated water. This is mainly due to
the trihalomethanes and other disinfection by-products, which are by-products
of chlorination. Trihalomethanes are carcinogens, and have been the topic of
concern in chlorinated drinking water. Chlorinated water has been associated
with increased risk of bladder, colon and rectal cancer. In the case of
bladder cancer, the risk may be doubled. Although there are concerns about
carcinogens in drinking water, Health Canada's Laboratory Centre for Disease
Control says that the benefits of chlorinated water in controlling infectious
diseases outweigh the risks associated with chlorination and would not be
enough to justify its discontinuation. In Europe, however, chorination has
been discontinued in many communities.

**Harnessing the Sun: Passive Solar Water Heating for Homes**  

In an era of rising energy costs and growing environmental concerns, homeowners are increasingly seeking ways to reduce reliance on conventional energy sources. One of the most accessible and effective methods is the installation of passive solar water heating systems. These systems use the sun’s abundant energy to provide hot water for domestic use, offering both economic and ecological benefits.  

### How Passive Solar Water Heating Works  

At the heart of a passive solar water heating system are roof-mounted solar collectors. These collectors are typically flat panels or evacuated tubes designed to absorb sunlight and transfer that energy to water or a heat-transfer fluid. Unlike active systems, which rely on pumps and controllers, passive designs use the natural movement of heated water—through thermosiphon principles or integrated collector-storage units—to circulate between the collector and a storage tank.  

In a typical thermosiphon setup, the solar collector is positioned below an insulated storage tank. As water in the collector warms, it becomes less dense and rises into the tank, while cooler water from the tank flows downward into the collector to be heated. This process continues as long as sunlight is available, requiring no mechanical intervention.  

### Design Considerations for Residential Buildings  

For maximum efficiency, collectors should be oriented toward true south (in the Northern Hemisphere) or true north (in the Southern Hemisphere), with a tilt angle roughly equal to the latitude of the location. The roof’s structural integrity must be assessed to ensure it can support the weight of the collector and the storage tank, especially when filled with water.  

The storage tank is insulated to retain heat, allowing homeowners to access hot water even during cloudy periods or at night. In colder climates, systems may include freeze protection measures, such as drain-back designs or antifreeze solutions in a closed-loop heat exchanger.  

### Benefits Beyond Energy Savings  

Passive solar water heating systems require minimal maintenance due to their simple design and lack of moving parts. This reliability translates into lower operating costs over the system’s lifespan. Additionally, because these systems draw energy directly from the sun, they produce no greenhouse gas emissions during operation, helping to reduce a household’s carbon footprint.  

For households with high hot water demand—such as those with multiple occupants—solar water heating can significantly offset utility bills. Over time, the savings can help recoup installation costs, making it a sound long-term investment.  

### Integration with Existing Infrastructure  

Many homeowners choose to integrate passive solar systems with conventional water heaters. In this hybrid arrangement, the solar-heated water pre-feeds the conventional unit, meaning the backup heater requires less energy to bring water to the desired temperature. This approach ensures a consistent supply of hot water while maximizing solar contributions.  

Retrofitting is possible for many existing homes, though it requires careful planning to route plumbing between the collectors and the storage tank. In new construction, incorporating passive solar heating into the design phase allows for optimal placement and integration.  

### Environmental Impact and Wider Adoption  

The adoption of passive solar water heating contributes to broader sustainability goals by reducing dependence on fossil fuels and lowering peak electricity demand. In regions with high solar insolation, these systems can supply 50–80% of a household’s annual hot water needs, dramatically cutting energy consumption.  

Government incentives, rebates, and tax credits in many areas further encourage installation. As awareness grows, more homeowners are recognizing that solar water heating is not only an environmentally responsible choice but also a practical one.  

### Conclusion  

Passive solar water heating systems offer a straightforward, low-maintenance solution to meet residential hot water needs using renewable energy. By harnessing the sun’s power through roof-mounted collectors and insulated storage tanks, households can reduce utility costs and environmental impact simultaneously. With careful design and proper installation, these systems can serve as a reliable, sustainable component of modern living—turning rooftops into silent, efficient providers of one of life’s essential resources.

gases. The gases comprise molecules that are evaporated from the electrolyte
and binder components. The metal alloy can be separated through

mixture of metals aluminum, manganese and lithium can either be reclaimed by

very versatile and relatively safe. Because there is no pre-sorting needed, it
can work with a wide variety of batteries. In addition, because the whole cell
is burnt, the metal from the current collectors could help the smelting

**E-Commerce Grocery Platforms: A Decade of Expansion and Innovation**  

Over the past ten years, the grocery industry has undergone a profound transformation driven by the rapid growth of e-commerce platforms. What began as a niche service in select metropolitan areas has evolved into a global phenomenon, reshaping the way consumers source and purchase food. This shift has been fueled by technological innovation, strategic investments from major retailers, and changing consumer preferences toward convenience and customization.  

**Early Development and Market Entry**  
In the early 2010s, online grocery shopping was still in its infancy in most regions, limited largely to pilot programs or specialized services targeting urban professionals. Companies like FreshDirect in the United States and Ocado in the United Kingdom were among the pioneers, building dedicated distribution centers and proprietary delivery logistics. The entry of Amazon into the grocery sector through AmazonFresh marked a turning point, signaling that e-commerce giants saw significant potential in food retail. Around the same time, subscription-based meal-kit providers began to emerge, leveraging direct-to-consumer fulfillment models that bypassed traditional retail channels.  

**Technological Innovations in Ordering and Fulfillment**  
Advances in mobile applications, personalized recommendation algorithms, and inventory management systems played a critical role in scaling grocery e-commerce. Retailers invested heavily in real-time stock tracking, ensuring that consumers could see accurate availability before placing orders. Geolocation services enabled tighter delivery windows, while automated warehouses and robotic picking systems increased order accuracy and speed. Innovations such as click-and-collect services allowed customers to order online and pick up groceries curbside, blending the benefits of digital convenience with the immediacy of in-person shopping.  

For subscription-based platforms, technology was equally transformative. Integrated recipe planning, portion control algorithms, and predictive demand modeling allowed companies to optimize ingredient sourcing and reduce supply chain inefficiencies. These systems also supported rapid seasonal menu rotation, keeping offerings fresh and engaging for subscribers.  

**Global Adoption Trends**  
North America and Western Europe led early adoption, driven by high internet penetration rates, dense urban populations, and consumer openness to new retail formats. In Asia, growth accelerated in the mid-2010s, particularly in China, where platforms like JD.com and Alibaba’s Hema Fresh combined online ordering with experiential retail spaces. Emerging markets in Latin America and parts of Africa have seen more recent expansion, often facilitated by mobile-first platforms that operate with leaner infrastructure.  

The COVID-19 pandemic served as a catalyst for widespread adoption, as lockdowns and safety concerns made online grocery shopping a necessity for millions. This surge in demand prompted both established supermarkets and new entrants to scale up digital capabilities, invest in contactless delivery technologies, and expand product ranges to include fresh produce, prepared meals, and specialty goods.  

**Competitive Landscape and Key Players**  
The competitive environment has diversified over the decade. Traditional supermarket chains such as Walmart and Tesco have integrated robust e-commerce channels alongside their physical stores. Pure-play digital grocers like Instacart have established partnerships with multiple retailers, acting as intermediaries between customers and brick-and-mortar outlets. Subscription meal-kit companies, including Blue Apron, HelloFresh, and Green Chef, have carved out a distinct niche by offering curated culinary experiences with pre-portioned ingredients.  

Strategic mergers and acquisitions have reshaped the market, with large players acquiring technology startups to enhance their platforms. For example, Kroger’s acquisition of Ocado’s automated warehouse technology expanded its fulfillment capabilities, while Amazon’s purchase of Whole Foods provided a hybrid model blending physical retail with advanced digital infrastructure.  

**Consumer Behavior and Future Outlook**  
Consumer adoption trends indicate a growing preference for flexibility and personalization. Shoppers increasingly expect seamless integration between online and offline experiences, such as the ability to modify orders in real time or combine delivery with in-store pickups. Sustainability is also emerging as a key factor influencing purchasing decisions, prompting companies to explore eco-friendly packaging solutions and localized sourcing to reduce environmental impacts.  

Looking ahead, analysts predict continued growth in e-commerce grocery sales, with emerging technologies like AI-driven demand forecasting, drone delivery, and blockchain-based supply chain transparency enhancing efficiency and trust. As competition intensifies, platforms will likely differentiate themselves through specialized offerings—ranging from hyper-local farm-to-door services to global gourmet ingredient sourcing—while balancing operational scale with responsiveness to evolving consumer expectations.  

In summary, the past decade has seen e-commerce grocery platforms transition from niche experiments to integral components of the global food retail ecosystem. This expansion, underpinned by technological innovation and shifting consumer habits, is poised to continue shaping how people access and experience food in the years ahead.

**Rethinking Grass Management in Permaculture: A Guide to Robotic Lawn Mowers**  

In permaculture design, one of the ongoing challenges is balancing low-maintenance systems with the needs of plant health, soil integrity, and aesthetics. While traditional approaches often involve grazing animals, mulching, or manual mowing, an increasing number of practitioners are turning to robotic lawn mowers as a quiet, energy-efficient, and non-disruptive solution for grass management. These machines offer a consistent way to maintain groundcover height, reduce labor, and integrate seamlessly into diverse garden layouts without introducing additional biological variables.  

---

### Why Consider Robotic Lawn Mowers in Permaculture?  

Permaculture emphasizes working with nature, but it also values tools that reduce human effort while preserving ecological function. Robotic mowers, unlike conventional gas-powered equipment, operate on rechargeable batteries, emit no direct exhaust, and can be programmed to work during off-peak hours. This makes them compatible with the permaculture principle of energy efficiency.  

Additionally, their quiet operation reduces disturbance to wildlife and human inhabitants, and their frequent, light cutting promotes a dense turf layer that prevents soil erosion. For food forests and perennial beds bordered by grassy zones, a robotic mower can keep paths and open spaces accessible without compacting soil through heavy foot or machine traffic.  

---

### Key Features to Compare  

**1. Battery Capacity and Charging Systems**  
Battery life determines how much area a mower can handle on a single charge. Entry-level models may handle 0.25 acres with 2–3 hours of mowing per day, while high-end units can manage over an acre with larger lithium-ion packs. Some models return automatically to their docking station when the battery runs low, resuming work after recharging. Solar-assisted docking stations are emerging, appealing to off-grid or low-energy setups.  

**2. Programming and Scheduling Options**  
Advanced robotic mowers allow highly customizable schedules, letting you set mowing times for specific zones. This can be particularly useful in a permaculture garden where certain areas—such as pollinator strips—should be left untouched during bloom periods. Some units integrate with smartphone apps, enabling remote monitoring and adjustments, while others use onboard controls for simple, set-and-forget operation.  

**3. Cutting Height and Mulching Ability**  
Maintaining the right grass height supports soil moisture retention and root health. Most robotic mowers offer adjustable cutting heights, often from 0.8 to 2.5 inches. Since these mowers operate frequently, they produce fine clippings that act as natural mulch, returning nutrients to the soil without creating visible thatch layers.  

**4. Navigation and Obstacle Detection**  
Boundary wires are still the most common way to define mowing zones, though newer models incorporate GPS-assisted mapping for more flexible layouts. Obstacle detection sensors help avoid collisions with garden beds, young trees, or trellises. In a permaculture context, where plantings may be irregular, look for models with advanced navigation to prevent damage to diverse plant species.  

---

### Comparing Popular Models  

- **Husqvarna Automower 430X** – Known for its GPS navigation and ability to handle complex terrain, this model suits larger permaculture properties. It offers weather resistance and a robust battery life for up to 0.8 acres.  
- **Worx Landroid WR155** – A mid-range option with app-based control, customizable mowing schedules, and a decent battery for medium-sized gardens.  
- **Robomow RS630** – Features wider cutting decks for faster coverage, making it efficient for open areas adjacent to food forest plantings.  
- **Gardena Sileno City** – Compact and quiet, ideal for smaller or more intricate spaces, with reliable obstacle detection and a user-friendly interface.  

---

### Integration Tips for Permaculture Gardens  

1. **Define Boundaries Clearly** – Use boundary wires or GPS mapping to ensure the mower stays in intended areas, avoiding sensitive plantings.  
2. **Segment Work Zones** – Program the mower to focus on paths, clearings, and gathering areas, leaving wildflower patches and cover crops untouched.  
3. **Work with Seasonal Cycles** – Adjust mowing schedules to accommodate flowering times, seed dispersal, or seasonal rest periods for certain groundcovers.  
4. **Pair with Mulching and Groundcovers** – Use the mower to manage grass height while allowing low-growing herbs and clovers to flourish in between mowings.  

---

### Conclusion  

Robotic lawn mowers provide a modern, low-impact approach to grass management that aligns well with permaculture principles of efficiency, minimal disturbance, and system integration. By carefully selecting a model with the right battery capacity, programming flexibility, and navigation capabilities, it’s possible to maintain healthy, accessible grassy zones without mechanical noise, fossil fuel use, or intensive manual labor. For practitioners seeking to streamline maintenance while keeping ecological integrity intact, these devices represent a compelling tool in the permaculture toolkit.

**Advances in Edible Packaging from Seaweed Extracts and Rice Starch: Production, Stability, and Consumer Acceptance**  

**Abstract**  
Edible packaging derived from renewable biopolymers offers a promising avenue for reducing dependence on single-use plastics in the food industry. Recent developments in the use of seaweed extracts and rice starch have demonstrated favorable mechanical properties, biodegradability, and functional performance for food preservation. This paper reviews current production methodologies, evaluates shelf-life stability under various storage conditions, and examines consumer acceptance of these innovations. Findings indicate that seaweed–rice starch composites can be formulated to achieve competitive tensile strength, moisture resistance, and palatability, though optimization of barrier properties and scalability remains an ongoing challenge. Consumer studies suggest growing willingness to adopt edible packaging, contingent on sensory quality and perceived safety.  

**1. Introduction**  
Single-use plastic packaging contributes significantly to environmental pollution and resource depletion, prompting research into sustainable alternatives. Edible packaging, defined as a consumable film or coating applied directly to food products, has gained attention for its potential to eliminate post-consumption waste entirely [1]. Biopolymers sourced from marine and agricultural resources—particularly seaweed extracts such as agar, carrageenan, and alginate, combined with rice starch—offer functional properties suitable for diverse food applications. This paper synthesizes recent progress in the formulation, processing, and evaluation of seaweed–rice starch edible packaging, with emphasis on industrial viability and consumer response.  

**2. Production Methods**  
Seaweed extracts provide a polysaccharide matrix with film-forming capability, while rice starch contributes to mechanical strength and modulates barrier properties [2]. Common production techniques include:  

- **Solution casting**: Dissolving seaweed extract and rice starch in water, plasticizers (e.g., glycerol) added to improve flexibility; the solution is cast and dried at controlled temperatures.  
- **Extrusion**: Thermo-mechanical processing of blended biopolymers into thin films, enabling continuous production lines.  
- **Hybrid processes**: Incorporation of natural antimicrobials or antioxidants during mixing to enhance preservation.  

Optimization of polymer ratios and processing parameters directly influences tensile strength, elongation at break, and water vapor transmission rate (WVTR). Studies report that blending rice starch with agar at 30–50% ratios can reduce brittleness without compromising transparency [3].  

**3. Shelf-Life Stability**  
Shelf-life performance of edible packaging depends on moisture sensitivity, microbial resistance, and structural integrity during storage. Seaweed–rice starch films typically exhibit higher WVTR than synthetic plastics, necessitating modification via crosslinking agents or lipid incorporation to improve barrier properties [4]. Temperature and relative humidity significantly affect mechanical stability; films stored at 25 °C and 50% RH maintain integrity for up to six months, while higher humidity accelerates degradation [5]. Antimicrobial additives, such as essential oils, have been shown to extend shelf-life by inhibiting microbial growth on the packaging surface.  

**4. Consumer Acceptance**  
Consumer adoption of edible packaging hinges on sensory attributes (taste, odor, texture), cultural perceptions, and trust in safety standards. Surveys in Southeast Asia and Europe indicate a positive inclination toward seaweed-based edible films, particularly for snack and confectionery applications [6]. However, respondents express concern over hygiene during handling and distribution, highlighting the need for protective secondary packaging or sealed manufacturing environments. Education on nutritional benefits and environmental impact enhances willingness to pay a premium for such products.  

**5. Challenges and Future Directions**  
While laboratory-scale results are promising, scaling production to meet commercial demands requires addressing:  

- **Barrier property enhancement** to match performance of current plastics in moisture- and oxygen-sensitive applications.  
- **Cost competitiveness** through efficient sourcing of raw materials and energy-saving processing techniques.  
- **Regulatory frameworks** ensuring safety, labeling, and allergen disclosure.  

Emerging research explores nanocellulose reinforcement, enzymatic modification of starch, and integration of bioactive compounds to expand functionality. Collaboration between material scientists, food technologists, and industry stakeholders will be critical for mainstream adoption.  

**6. Conclusion**  
Edible packaging made from seaweed extracts and rice starch represents a viable strategy for mitigating the environmental impact of single-use plastics, combining biodegradability with functional food preservation. Continued innovation in material formulation, processing efficiency, and consumer engagement will determine the extent to which these solutions can be integrated into global food supply chains.

This has led to a revival of hemp farming, particularly after the European Union, the United States, and several other nations legalized its production under strict regulations to maintain low THC levels ( Ramshankar et al., 2025, Tedeschi et al., 2020). In 2021, the global industrial hemp market was estimated at around USD 4.13 billion, with projections showing a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 16.8 % from 2022 to 2030. The rising demand for industrial hemp across multiple industries continues to drive market expansion ( Industrial Hemp Market Size & Share, Industry Report, 2030; Burton et al., 2022). In recent years, hemp fiber has been increasingly used construction engineering ( Ramshankar et al., 2025, Nazari and Woods, 2025, Arehart et al., 2020) and in natural fiber-reinforced polymer composites for the automotive due to its lightweight properties, sustainability, cost-effectiveness, and environmental benefits ( Srivastava et al., 2025; Musa and Onwualu, 2024 ; Sultan et al., 2024; Panaitescu et al., 2020; Tanasa et al., 2020 ; Sepe et al., 2018). Despite these benefits, hemp, being a lignocellulosic fiber, offers poor spinnability. Researchers have been persistently working on softening it through enzyme and chemical treatments; but hemp still cannot be spun into yarn solely using traditional spinning methods. To convert into yarn, hemp has been blended with other fibers like cotton ( Ling et al., 2024; Ahirwar and Behera, 2022; Özşahin et al., 2022; Kozłowski et al., 2013), cotton and viscose ( Li et al., 2023), flax ( Okur, 2021), nylon ( Ling et al., 2023), and PET ( Zhang et al., 2014) to produce yarns in ring, and rotor spinning systems. **The Evolution of Lithium-Ion Battery Technology in Consumer Electronics**  

Over the past three decades, lithium-ion batteries have transformed the landscape of portable consumer electronics. From the first commercially available lithium-ion cells in the early 1990s to the sophisticated energy storage units in today’s smartphones and laptops, the technology has undergone continuous refinement. The history of these advancements reveals a consistent pursuit of higher energy density, faster charging capabilities, and improved safety measures—each driven by the demands of increasingly powerful and compact electronic devices.  

**Early Development and Commercialization**  
Lithium-ion technology emerged from research in the 1970s and 1980s, with Sony introducing the first commercial lithium-ion battery in 1991. These early cells represented a leap forward from nickel-cadmium and nickel-metal hydride batteries, offering significantly higher energy density and lighter weight. The chemistry relied on a lithium cobalt oxide (LiCoO₂) cathode and a graphite anode, enabling higher voltages and longer runtimes for portable devices.  

In the early generations, energy density improvements were incremental, often constrained by safety concerns such as thermal runaway—a chain reaction where excessive heat leads to battery failure. Nevertheless, the ability to store more energy per unit mass became a defining advantage, allowing electronics manufacturers to design sleeker, more capable devices.  

**Advances in Energy Density**  
By the mid-2000s, material science breakthroughs led to alternative cathode chemistries, including lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO₄) and lithium nickel manganese cobalt oxide (NMC). These offered more stable thermal properties and higher capacity, enabling laptops to run longer between charges and smartphones to support increasingly complex applications. Silicon-based anodes began to replace or supplement graphite, further boosting storage capacity by accommodating more lithium ions during charging.  

Manufacturers also refined electrode designs, electrolyte formulations, and separator materials to pack more power into smaller spaces. Today’s flagship smartphones often feature batteries exceeding 250 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg), compared to less than 150 Wh/kg in early 2000s models. This jump in density has been essential to supporting high-resolution displays, advanced processors, and multi-sensor camera systems without sacrificing portability.  

**Charging Speed Innovations**  
As energy density grew, consumer expectations shifted toward faster recharging. Early lithium-ion batteries required several hours for a full charge, but modern designs—combined with advanced charging protocols—can achieve 50–80% capacity in under 30 minutes.  

Key innovations have included refined electrolyte additives to support higher charge rates without degrading electrodes, and improved battery management systems (BMS) that regulate current flow, voltage, and temperature during charging. USB Power Delivery and proprietary fast-charging standards from major electronics brands have leveraged these advances to deliver rapid replenishment without compromising cell longevity.  

**Safety Enhancements**  
Safety has remained a central focus throughout lithium-ion’s evolution. Incidents of overheating or fire in early devices prompted extensive research into preventing short circuits and managing heat. Modern cells employ robust separators that resist puncture, shutdown mechanisms that halt ion flow in unsafe conditions, and carefully engineered venting systems.  

In addition, contemporary BMS software constantly monitors cell health, adjusting charging and discharging rates to minimize risk. Some manufacturers have incorporated solid-state electrolytes in prototype devices, which promise even greater safety by eliminating flammable liquid components.  

**Integration into Consumer Electronics Design**  
Advancements in lithium-ion technology have influenced the broader design of smartphones and laptops. Higher energy density allows manufacturers to allocate more internal space to other components, such as processors, cooling systems, or enhanced audio hardware. Faster charging aligns with the mobile lifestyles of users, reducing downtime and improving usability.  

Furthermore, improved cycle life—often exceeding 800–1000 full charge cycles—ensures that devices can maintain acceptable battery performance for several years, extending their practical lifespan and reducing the frequency of replacements.  

**Looking Forward**  
Research continues into next-generation lithium-ion cells and alternatives like lithium-sulfur and solid-state batteries. Goals include surpassing current density limits, achieving even faster charging without degradation, and further enhancing safety. For consumer electronics, these improvements promise smaller, lighter devices with longer runtimes and more flexible usage patterns.  

The trajectory of lithium-ion battery technology illustrates a remarkable interplay between chemistry, engineering, and user demand. From the bulky, short-lived batteries of early mobile devices to the sleek, high-capacity cells of modern electronics, each stage of innovation has reshaped what is possible in portable computing and communication. As research progresses, the boundaries of performance, convenience, and safety will continue to expand, ensuring that energy storage remains a cornerstone of technological advancement in everyday life.
